bottomLine: On His last night, before He crossed the brook into the garden, Jesus lifted His eyes and prayed. The hour had come. The Father had given Him authority over all flesh, and He uses it to give eternal life to all the Father gave Him. Eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent, and it starts the day you believe. The Son finished the work. Stop working for a payout. Know Him.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, the way the Son lifted His on the last night. Lift them past the clock on the wall and the bills on the counter. Lift them past the grave you have been treating as the place where real life finally starts. Lift them all the way to the Father, because the Son you trust is with Him now, and He went there by way of the hour that saved you.

The dust has told you eternal life is a pension, paid out later to men whose records hold up. It has told you God is someone to know about and keep happy, like a foreman up on the hill. You have worked under that lie for years. You have gone to church under it, prayed under it, and come home tired under it. It has turned faith into one more chore and left your soul as dry as a stock tank in August.

But hear what the Son told His Father with the cross a day away. This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ. He has authority over all flesh, and He uses it to give. He came down to the earth and did every hour of the Father’s work without a slip. I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do. The next day He carried it to the cross. Then He came up out of the grave in the same body they buried and went home to the glory He had before the world existed — a Man in heaven, with nail scars in His hands.

So carry one sentence into this week. When you wake, it is true: eternal life is knowing Him, and you have it. When the job goes sideways, it is still true: the Son’s work did not go sideways. When you stand at a grave, it is true again: the life He gave you does not end in that ground. The Father gave you to the Son. The Son gives you eternal life. He has not asked you to climb up to Him. He came down, did the work, and went home ahead of you. And He gives you Himself, to know and to be known by, starting at your own kitchen sink this morning.
closingVerse: This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.
carry: Jesus said eternal life is knowing the only true God and the Son He sent, starting now; what part of your ordinary week have you left outside that knowing, as if life will not begin until later?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Somewhere along the way you picked up the idea that God saves a man and then steps back to see if he can hold on. The rescue was His. The keeping is yours. So you grip. You grit your teeth against the old sins and promise to do better on Monday. Most weeks you lose a little ground, and you start to wonder if you will be the one who slips all the way off.

The dust has two answers for a man in that spot, and both are lies. The first says the only way to stay clean is to hide — keep away from the crew, the town, the people who do not know God, and build a high wall around your house. The second says the only way to live in the world is to look like it — laugh at the jokes, spend like the neighbors, keep your faith in a drawer at home. One road leaves a man proud and alone. The other leaves him dirty. Both leave him tired.

Under all of it, the dust says no one is praying for you. You are a man on your own with weak hands and a long road. You have prayed it, maybe without knowing whose words they were: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Look at the last four words. The man who prayed them did not ask for a stronger grip. He asked to be made alive by what God says.
That is how God keeps and cleans His people in John 17. Jesus prays for His own, and He asks His Father to do it by one means: Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth.

sections.heading: The Men in the Room
pulls: The dust says God saves a man and then steps back to see if he can hold on. Jesus says the Father gave you to Him, that He has kept His own, and that He prays for them to be kept.
paras: The Son has prayed for Himself. Now He turns to the men around Him. Judas has already gone out into the night. Peter has been told that before the rooster crows he will deny his Master three times. All of them have been told they will scatter and leave Him alone. Within hours every word of that will come true.

This is what Jesus prays over those men, out loud, while they listen. He does not pray that they will be strong. He prays that the Father will keep them, guard them from the evil one, and make them holy by His word. Read it as one of them. A little further on He will widen the prayer to everyone who believes through their word, and that includes you. But first hear what He asks for the men closest to Him, because what He asks for them He asks for all His own.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: GIVEN OUT OF THE WORLD
paras: I revealed your name to the people whom you have given me out of the world. They were yours, and you have given them to me. Before these men ever followed Jesus, they belonged to the Father. He gave them to His Son. That is where their story starts, and it is where yours starts too. Your faith did not begin with your choice. It began with the Father’s gift.

Then Jesus adds, They have kept your word. These men? They argued about who was greatest. They missed His meaning over and over. Within hours they would run. Yet the Son speaks of them to His Father with no sneer in His voice. He does not hide their weakness, and He does not define them by it.

Here is why. For the words which you have given me I have given to them, and they received them, and knew for sure that I came from you. They have believed that you sent me. Watch the chain. The Father gave the words to the Son. The Son gave them to the men. The men received them. Their faith was not strong because they were strong. It was real because the word was real.

That is good news for a man whose faith shakes. Jesus does not measure you by the night you are about to have. He looks at what you have received from Him. If you have received His word and believed that the Father sent Him, the Son counts you as His own. He speaks well of you to His Father, and He does it with your worst night in full view.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: I PRAY FOR THEM
paras: I pray for them. I don’t pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. Do not hear coldness in this. In this same prayer Jesus sends these men into the world, and John has already told you that God so loved the world that He gave His Son. The door of the gospel stands open to every man. But on this night, at this hour, the Son prays for His own the way a father on his deathbed prays for his own sons, by name.

That is a particular love, and it is the kind you want. A general good will toward mankind does not keep a man on a hard night. A Shepherd who knows His sheep and prays for them does. He knows which of His men is weakest, and He prays for that one too. I know my own, and I’m known by my own.

All things that are mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them. Jesus is glorified in eleven men who will fail Him before dawn. He is not glorified in them because of their record. He is glorified in them because they are the Father’s gift, and He is about to save them at the cost of His own blood.

And the praying did not stop that night. The writer of Hebrews says the risen Christ is also able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, seeing that he lives forever to make intercession for them. Right now, while you read this, the Son prays for His own. You are not on your own.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: KEPT IN HIS NAME
pulls: None of His own is lost. Not the ones who ran, not the one who denied Him by the fire, not you. The Son who kept them in His Father’s name has never yet dropped a man the Father gave Him.
paras: I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them through your name which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are. He is leaving. They are staying. So He hands them over to His Father’s keeping, the way a man leaving on a long haul puts his family in the care of a brother he trusts.

While I was with them in the world, I kept them in your name. I have kept those whom you have given me. None of them is lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled. Look at that record. Years of storms and crowds and enemies, and not one of the Father’s gift was lost. Judas was lost. He ate bread at the Lord’s table and went out into the night. The Scripture had said it would be so, and still the betrayal was his own. His sin did not catch God short, and God’s plan did not excuse his sin. Leave it there.

But do not miss the main thing, which is the keeping. The Son does not lose what the Father gives Him. He said it in plain words months before: I give eternal life to them. They will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.

But now I come to you, and I say these things in the world, that they may have my joy made full in themselves. He prays out loud so His men will hear it and have His joy. A man who knows he is kept can be glad even on the worst night of his life.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: NOT OUT, BUT SENT
paras: I have given them your word. The world hated them, because they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world. The word sets a man apart, and the world feels it. Then the request: I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one. Jesus does not ask for a wall. He asks for a keeper. The answer to the world is not to hide from it or to blend into it. It is to be kept in it.

Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth. Here is how the Father keeps His people clean. Not by willpower. Not by distance. By His word. The same word that brought you life now sets you apart and makes you holy, a little at a time, the way water wears down stone. You do not sanctify yourself. You sit under the word, and the Father does it.
As you sent me into the world, even so I have sent them into the world. Set apart, then sent back in. Kept on the job, not pulled off it.

For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth. This is the root of it all. The Son set Himself apart for the cross. He gave Himself up for His own, and He did it for their sakes. Your holiness grows out of His sacrifice the way a crop grows out of seed already in the ground. Before He asks anything of you, He gave Himself for you. His setting apart came first. Yours follows, and it cannot fail, because it hangs on His.

stations.verse: For the words which you have given me I have given to them, and they received them, and knew for sure that I came from you. They have believed that you sent me.
stations.question: Jesus said His men received them, and knew for sure that I came from you — sure because of the words He gave, not their nerve; what word of His can I stand on when my faith feels thin?
stations.gloss: truly; surely, for certain
body: Alēthōs is an adverb meaning truly or surely. It marks a thing as so, not just said. It shows up in eighteen verses. The crowd says of Jesus, This is truly the prophet. Jesus tells the Jews who believed Him, If you remain in my word, then you are truly my disciples.

In 17:8 the WEB renders it knew for sure. Jesus says it of men who would scatter within hours. Their sureness did not come from their nerve. It came from the words: they received them. Paul thanks God for the same thing in Thessalonica, for men who took the message not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God.
The dust says you only believe as much as you feel. Jesus says a man who has received His word knows for sure — even on the night his legs give out.
stations.live: Write down one thing you know for sure because God has said it, not because you feel it. Read it aloud on the morning you feel least sure: ‘He said it. I have received it. It is so.’

stations.verse: All things that are mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.
stations.question: Of eleven men who would fail Him that night, Jesus told the Father, yours are mine, and I am glorified in them; what failure of mine have I let convince me that I no longer belong to Him?
stations.gloss: your, yours; what belongs to you
body: Sos is the plain word for yours — what belongs to the one spoken to. It is used in twenty-two verses. In Luke a father tells his angry older son, all that is mine is yours. On the Mount of Olives Jesus prays, not my will, but yours, be done.

Here the word sits in the middle of an exchange between Father and Son: yours are mine. The men in the room belong to both, held between them. John uses the same word again a few verses on, in this week’s key verse — Your word is truth. The people are the Father’s, and the word that makes them holy is His too.

The dust says you belong to whatever you did last — your record, your sin, your debts. The Son says you belong to the Father and to Him. A man owned like that is not for sale, and he is not up for grabs.
stations.live: Write ‘Yours are mine’ on a card and tape it where you see your own name — the mailbox, the paycheck stub, the lunch pail. Each time you see it this week, remember whose you are, and say so.

stations.verse: While I was with them in the world, I kept them in your name. I have kept those whom you have given me. None of them is lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.
stations.question: Jesus told His Father, I have kept those whom you have given me, losing none but the son of destruction; what does that record say to my fear of slipping away?
stations.gloss: destruction, ruin; perishing, loss
body: Apōleia means destruction, loss, perishing. It can mean plain waste — when the ointment was poured out, the disciples asked, Why this waste? In its heaviest sense it is the loss of eternal life, the opposite of salvation. Seventeen verses carry it.

Jesus calls Judas the son of destruction, a phrase Paul uses again for the man of sin. Judas ate bread at Jesus’ table and went out into the night. He was not lost because the Son failed to keep him. He was lost as the Scripture said, by his own betrayal.

The dust says you could be next, that Christ will hold you only as long as you hold Him. Hear the same verse: I have kept those whom you have given me. Hebrews says it of all His own: we are not of those who shrink back to destruction.
stations.live: When the fear of falling away keeps you awake, read John 17:12 and 10:28–29 side by side. Then pray: ‘You have kept me. You will not lose what the Father gave You.’

stations.verse: While I was with them in the world, I kept them in your name. I have kept those whom you have given me. None of them is lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.
stations.question: Jesus said even Judas’ betrayal at His own table happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled; what hard turn in my own life am I still reading as if God had looked away?
stations.gloss: a writing; the Scripture
body: Graphē means a writing, something written down. In the New Testament it names the holy writings, the Scriptures. In the plural it means the whole of them; in the singular it usually points to one passage. You will find it in forty-nine verses.

Here it is singular, and John has already told you which passage. At the supper Jesus said, that the Scripture may be fulfilled, ‘He who eats bread with me has lifted up his heel against me.’ Those words are from Psalm 41:9. The betrayal did not catch God short. It was written down long before Judas was born. As Jesus said, the Scripture can’t be broken.
The dust says your life runs on chance, and when a friend turns on you, God must have looked away. Jesus walked into His worst night with the Scripture in His mouth. The word that held Him holds you.
stations.live: This week, when something goes wrong, open your Bible before you open your mouth. Find one verse that speaks to it, read it twice, and say: ‘The Scripture can’t be broken.’

stations.verse: I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one.
stations.question: Jesus did not ask the Father to take His men out of the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one; where am I trying to stay safe by pulling away instead of trusting His keeping?
stations.gloss: bad, evil; the evil one
body: Ponēros comes from a verb meaning to toil, and in older Greek it could mean worn down by labor, or painful. In the New Testament it means bad or worthless, and then wicked. With the article it names Satan, the evil one. It stands in seventy-two verses.

Jesus taught His men to pray, deliver us from the evil one. Now He prays it for them Himself. He does not ask for a fence around them. He asks His Father to keep them while they stay in the world. Paul leans on the same keeping: the Lord is faithful, who will establish you and guard you from the evil one.
The dust says the enemy is stronger than you, and that much is true. It says you must hide or lose, and that is a lie. The Son asked His Father to keep you, and the Father hears the Son.
stations.live: Pray Matthew 6:13 each morning this week with John 17:15 open beside it. Then go out to wherever the world is — the crew, the feed store, the ball field — and say: ‘I am kept. I am sent.’

practices.title: LET THE WORD DO THE WORK
practices.body: Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth. The Father’s way of making you holy is His word, not your willpower. So give the word room. Read John 17 every day this week, start to finish. Then pick one line and carry it through the day. Say it on the drive, at the bench, over the sink. You are not cramming for a test. You are being washed, and the Father is the one doing the washing.

practices.title: REMEMBER WHO IS PRAYING
practices.body: When the old sin comes knocking this week — the screen at midnight, the temper, the cutting word to your wife — stop long enough to remember that the Son asked His Father to keep you from the evil one, and that he lives forever to make intercession for them. Say it aloud: ‘Christ is praying for me right now.’ Then turn from the thing, leaning on His prayer, not your resolve.

practices.title: GO BACK WHERE HE SENT YOU
practices.body: As you sent me into the world, even so I have sent them into the world. Name one place you have been pulling back from because the people there do not know Christ — the loading dock, your brother’s house, the neighbor you avoid. Go back in this week. Do one plain kindness there, and if the door opens, say one plain word about Jesus. You are sent, and you are kept while you go.

practices.title: RECEIVE WHAT HE GAVE THEM
practices.body: Jesus said of His men, they received them, and knew for sure. Sit down once this week for half an hour with your Bible and without your phone. Read John 14–17 straight through, the words He gave them that night. Write down one thing He said that you have been doubting. Then write under it: ‘He gave me this word. I receive it.’ Read what you wrote again on Sunday, before you go to church, and thank Him for it.

practices.title: PRAY FOR YOUR OWN BY NAME
practices.body: Jesus prayed for those the Father gave Him — that they would be kept, guarded, and made holy. Pray the same way for the people God has put in your care. Write down your wife, your children, the men you work beside. Under each name, write John 17:15 and 17:17 in your own words. Pray through the list every evening this week. Do not turn it into a speech. Short and plain is enough. You are not their keeper. You are asking the Keeper.

title: Sanctify Them in the Truth
subtitle: from dust to a people kept by His prayer
keyVerse: Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth.

passage.text: I revealed your name to the people whom you have given me out of the world. They were yours, and you have given them to me. They have kept your word.
Now they have known that all things whatever you have given me are from you,
for the words which you have given me I have given to them, and they received them, and knew for sure that I came from you. They have believed that you sent me.
I pray for them. I don’t pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.
All things that are mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.
I am no more in the world, but these are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them through your name which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are.
While I was with them in the world, I kept them in your name. I have kept those whom you have given me. None of them is lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.
But now I come to you, and I say these things in the world, that they may have my joy made full in themselves.
I have given them your word. The world hated them, because they are not of the world, even as I am not of the world.
I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one.
They are not of the world even as I am not of the world.
Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth.
As you sent me into the world, even so I have sent them into the world.
For their sakes I sanctify myself, that they themselves also may be sanctified in truth.

stationsIntro: These words were spoken over men who would fail Him before morning. Read them as one of those men, answer plainly, and let each Greek word turn you back to the One who prayed.
lifeIntro: On His last night, Jesus spent His breath on men who were about to fail Him. He asked His Father to keep them, to guard them from the evil one, and to make them holy by His word — and He set Himself apart for the cross so it would be so. You are not keeping yourself. These practices are for a man who is kept, learning to live like it.
lifePulls: Christ did not pray that His men would be taken out of the world. He prayed that they would be kept in it and made holy by the Father’s word. That prayer stands over you this week.
prayer: Father, Your Son prayed for His own on the night before the cross, and He prays for them still. Thank You that You gave me to Him, and that He has made Your name known to me. Thank You that He has kept every one You gave Him, and that none of His own is lost. Keep me through Your name this week, and keep me from the evil one. Do not take me out of the world; send me into it, and guard me while I go. Sanctify me in Your truth. Your word is truth. Forgive me for trying to make myself holy by my own strength, and for hiding when You sent me. Let the joy of Your Son be made full in me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, Your Son prayed for His own on the night before the cross, and He prays
for them still.
Thank You that You gave me to Him, and that He has made Your name known to
me.
Thank You that He has kept every one You gave Him, and that none of His own is
lost.
Keep me through Your name this week, and keep me from the evil one.
Do not take me out of the world; send me into it, and guard me while I go.
Sanctify me in Your truth. Your word is truth.
Forgive me for trying to make myself holy by my own strength, and for hiding
when You sent me.
Let the joy of Your Son be made full in me.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: On the night before the cross, Jesus prayed for eleven men who were about to fail Him. They were the Father’s gift to Him, and He had kept every one. He did not ask that they be taken out of the world. He asked that they be kept from the evil one and made holy by the truth: Your word is truth. He still prays for His own. Stop trying to keep yourself. Open the word and be kept.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and see who is praying for you. Not a friend who means well and forgets by Friday. Not a busy pastor working down a long list. Not a prayer chain that loses your name by Sunday. The Son of God, with the cross a day away, spent His breath on men like you. He named them as His Father’s gift. He told the Father He had kept them. He asked that they be kept still.

The dust has told you that once you are saved, the rest is up to you — hold on, grit your teeth, keep yourself clean, and hope you are not the one who slips. It has told you the only way to stay holy is to hide, and the only way to live in the world is to look like it. You have tried both roads. One left you proud and lonely. The other left you dirty. Both left you worn out, and neither one was ever the road He laid out for you.

But hear Him. I have kept those whom you have given me. He kept the man who would warm his hands at a fire in the high priest’s courtyard and say three times that he was not His disciple. He kept the ones who ran. Then He said, For their sakes I sanctify myself, and He meant the cross. He set Himself apart for it, went to it, and paid there for the sins of His own. He came back from the dead with the wounds still in His hands, and He went up to His Father to keep on praying. He lives forever to make intercession for them.

So go into the world this week as a man who is kept. When the evil one comes for you, remember whose prayer stands over you. When you feel unclean, open the book, because Your word is truth, and the Father uses it to wash you. When you fear you will be the one who falls away, look at the record. Not one of the Father’s gift has been lost from the Son’s hand. You were given. You are kept. You are being made holy by a word that does not lie. And the Son who prays for you has never once been refused by His Father.
closingVerse: Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth.
carry: Jesus asked His Father, Sanctify them in your truth. Your word is truth; where this week will you put yourself under the Father’s word and let it do the work your own willpower has never done?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There is a kind of loneliness a man carries into church and out again. He shakes hands at the door. He sits where he always sits. He knows the names of the men in the next pew and almost nothing of what they carry, and they know less about him. On the drive home he thinks what he has thought for years: this faith is between me and God, and God is busy.

The dust builds on that. It says the prayers of Jesus were for the men in the room that night — Peter, John, the eleven — and you came along too late to be named. It says the church is a crowd of strangers who will let you down, so keep your distance and your own counsel. And it says that when the end comes, the best you can hope for is to be let in at the back, tolerated, given a chair near the door.

Lie in that long enough and you stop expecting anything from God or from His people. Then the old line becomes your own: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) A man face-down in the dirt does not need a pep talk. He needs to hear what was said about him before he ever lifted his head.

John 17:20–26 is that word. Jesus is still praying, and His eyes go past the eleven, past the years, to you. He asks the Father to make you one with His people. Then He tells the Father what He wants: you, with Him, where He is.

sections.heading: Past the Eleven
pulls: The dust says the prayers of Jesus were for other men in another room. But before the arrest, the Son looked down the years and prayed for those who would believe in Him through the apostles’ word. That is you.
paras: This is the end of the long prayer Jesus prayed on the night He was betrayed. He has prayed for Himself, that the Father would glorify the Son. He has prayed for the eleven, that the Father would keep them and sanctify them in the truth. Now the circle widens. The very next sentence in John’s Gospel reads, When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron. These are the last words of the prayer, spoken with the arrest close at hand.

So read these seven verses as the words of a Man who knows what is coming and spends His last quiet breath on people He has not yet met. He does not ask that they become impressive. He asks that they be one, that the Father’s love be in them, and that they be with Him. Keep that order in view. What He asks for, He has already set about giving.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE PRAYER THAT REACHED YOU
paras: Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word. The eleven were in the room. You were not. You had not been born, and neither had your grandfather’s grandfather. Yet Jesus counted you in that night as surely as He counted Peter. If you believe in Him, you were on His lips before the soldiers came.

Notice how you were going to come to faith: through their word. Not through a feeling that rose in you on a good morning. Not through your own digging. The apostles would preach and write what they had seen and heard, and men would believe. John says it of his own book near the end: these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. The Gospel in your hands is part of the answer to this prayer. So is the man who first opened it to you — a father, a pastor, a friend at the feed store who would not leave you alone.

This is grace before it is anything else. Christ did not wait to see whether you would turn out worth praying for. He prayed, and the Father answered by drawing you to the Son. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. Your faith is real, and it is yours. But it was asked for before it was given.
And the praying did not stop that night. The risen Christ goes on speaking to the Father for His own. The prayer of John 17 is still going up, and you are in it.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: ONE AS THE FATHER AND SON ARE ONE
paras: That they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us. Look at the pattern Jesus sets for this oneness. It is God’s own life — the Father in the Son and the Son in the Father. Jesus asks that His people be one in us. You do not build this unity. You are drawn into it.

Then He tells you what He has already done toward it. The glory which you have given me, I have given to them; that they may be one, even as we are one. He has given it. The glory of the Son — His standing with the Father, His life, His name — is shared out to the men who believe. You and the brother you have not spoken to since the business meeting hold the same gift from the same hand. That is what makes you one, long before you like each other.

The unity is Christ’s gift. But you can deny it with your mouth. The side comment in the parking lot. The cold silence toward a brother who wronged you. The sneer at the church across the highway. None of that breaks what Christ has joined. It only hides it from the people watching.

And people are watching. That the world may believe that you sent me. The oneness of His people is meant to be seen. When men who would never share a meal anywhere else sit at one table, love one another, and hold the same truth, the world gets a look at something it cannot explain. Jesus said it at the supper: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: PERFECTED INTO ONE
pulls: The Father loves those who are in Christ with the love He has for His own Son. Not a smaller share. Not a portion measured out to the deserving. The same love, from before the foundation of the world.
paras: I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one. Here is how the glory gets from the Father to you. The Father is in the Son. The Son is in His people. There is no break in the line. When Christ says I in them, He is not describing a mood. He is telling you where He lives. He does not stop by on Sunday and leave by Monday noon. He stays.

The word for perfected is the same word Jesus used earlier in this prayer for His own work: I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do. It is the word for bringing a thing to its end. The One who finishes His work will finish His people. Your church is not finished. Neither are you, and you know it better than anyone in the pew beside you. But the oneness Jesus prays for is headed somewhere, and He is the one taking it there.

Then comes the line a man could read a hundred times and still not take in. That the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me. Even as. The Father loves those who are in Christ with the love He has for His own Son. Not a smaller share. Not a portion measured out to the deserving. The same love.

You have been loved by fathers who were tired, by bosses who wanted something, by friends who drifted off when the work dried up. This love does not drift. It is the love the Father has had for the Son from before the world began, and Christ asks that the world see it resting on you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: WITH ME WHERE I AM
paras: Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory. Up to now Jesus has been asking. Here He tells the Father what He wants. The night before the cross, His wish is for you. He wants you with Him. He wants you to see His glory, which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world.

Heaven is not a back room where you are put up with. It is the place where the Son wants you, and the Father always hears the Son. Jesus said so at Lazarus’ grave: I know that you always listen to me. The dust says you will be lucky to be let in. Christ says He wants you there. You know which of the two the Father will hear.

Righteous Father, the world hasn’t known you, but I knew you; and these knew that you sent me. Jesus calls on the Father as righteous. The world has not known Him. But the Son has, and the Son has shown Him to these men. So He finishes: I made known to them your name, and will make it known; that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.

And will make it known. The Son would make the Father’s name known as never before — on a cross before the next sundown, and then outside an empty tomb. The last thing He asks before He goes out to the soldiers is that the Father’s love be in you, and that He be in you. Then He gets up, crosses the brook, and walks out to make that prayer good.

stations.verse: I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one; that the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me.
stations.question: Jesus prayed I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one, so the world would see the Father’s love on His people; what would my coworkers see of that love in how I treat other believers?
stations.gloss: to bring to an end, finish; to make complete, perfect
body: Teleioō means to bring a thing to its end — to finish, to accomplish — and so to bring it to completeness, to perfect it. The New Testament has it in twenty-three verses. In John it first belongs to Jesus Himself: My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.

He uses it again in this prayer: I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do. Later in the same prayer the word falls on His people: that they may be perfected into one. Hebrews says it outright: by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. The finishing is His.

The dust says the unity of God’s people is a job nobody will ever finish. But teleioō is the word of a Workman who does not walk off a job half done. He finished the cross. He will finish His church, and you in it.
stations.live: Name the believer you have quietly written off. Sit with him this week — coffee, a ride, a word after church — and say to yourself on the way: ‘Christ is in him too, and He is not finished with him or with me.’

stations.verse: Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory, which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world.
stations.question: Jesus told His Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am; what do I expect at the end of my life, now that I know what Christ wants?
stations.gloss: to will, to wish, to desire
body: Thelō is the plain word for wanting — to will, to be willing, to wish, to desire. It is common, found in one hundred ninety-nine verses. Here it is followed by the thing wanted: that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am.

Mark uses the same word in Gethsemane: not what I desire, but what you desire. John has it earlier of the Son’s power: the Son also gives life to whom he desires. What the Son wants never pulls against the Father. On this night, what He wants is you — with Him, seeing His glory.

The dust says God puts up with you, and the best you can hope for at the end is a chair by the door. Thelō answers with the Son’s own wish, spoken to His Father the night before He died. He did not ask to tolerate you. He asked to have you.
stations.live: Write John 17:24 on a card and read it before you sleep each night this week. When the old fear of not being wanted rises, say it back: ‘The Son told His Father He wants me with Him.’

stations.verse: Righteous Father, the world hasn’t known you, but I knew you; and these knew that you sent me.
stations.question: Jesus told the Father, the world hasn’t known you, but I knew you; and these knew that you sent me; what do I know of the Righteous Father that I could only have learned through the Son He sent?
stations.gloss: righteous; just, giving each his due
body: Dikaios means righteous — what matches God’s own standard of right — and, more narrowly, just, giving each his due. In the Greek Old Testament it mostly renders the Hebrew word for a righteous man. It is in seventy-four verses, used of men, of God, and of Christ, Jesus Christ, the righteous.

John uses it in only three verses, and this is the one where it names the Father. Jesus calls Him Righteous Father in the same breath as He says the world has not known Him. The righteous God is no stranger to the Son, and through the Son He is no stranger to the men who believe.

The dust hears the word righteous and braces for the blow. But the Righteous Father has a righteous Son, who suffered for sins once, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring you to God. God’s justice no longer stands against you. It stands behind your pardon.
stations.live: Begin each prayer this week with Jesus’ own words, ‘Righteous Father,’ and then give the reason you can come near: ‘I come in the name of Jesus Christ, the righteous.’

stations.verse: I made known to them your name, and will make it known; that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.
stations.question: Jesus promised the Father, I made known to them your name, and will make it known; what part of the Father’s heart am I still slow to believe, though the Son has promised to keep showing Him to me?
stations.gloss: to make known
body: Gnōrizō is built on the common verb for knowing, and means to make known. In the Greek Old Testament it mostly renders the Hebrew word for causing someone to know. It occurs in twenty-three verses. John has it twice, both from Jesus: everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you, and here.

Jesus speaks of it in two tenses. I made known to them your name — every word and sign of His years with them. And will make it known — the cross, the empty tomb, the Spirit sent. Paul uses the same verb of God making known to us the mystery of his will. The Son is not done showing you the Father.
The dust says God is a locked door, and what you know of Him is all you will ever know. Gnōrizō says the One who opened the door is still opening it, as He promised.
stations.live: Read one chapter of John each day this week. Before you start, ask plainly: ‘Lord Jesus, You said You would make the Father known. Show Him to me here.’

stations.verse: I made known to them your name, and will make it known; that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.
stations.question: The last thing Jesus asks before He crosses the brook is that the love with which you loved me may be in them; where am I living as if the Father’s love for me were smaller than His love for His Son?
stations.gloss: love; goodwill that chooses its object
body: Agapē is love, goodwill. Outside the Bible and the writings of the church there is no clear example of the noun. The New Testament took it over from the Greek Old Testament and used it for the bond of love between God and man in Christ, and between men in Christ. It is a love that chooses its object. It appears in one hundred six verses.
Here it is the Father’s love for the Son — the love He had before the foundation of the world. And Jesus asks that this same love may be in them, and I in them. Where He lives, it lives.

The dust says love is rationed — earned on good weeks, cut off on bad ones. But the love Christ asks for you is the Father’s love for His Son, and nothing in all creation will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
stations.live: When you have failed this week and the old voice says you have lost God’s favor, say out loud: ‘The love the Father has for His Son is in me, because Christ is in me.’

practices.title: PRAY FOR THOSE WHO WILL BELIEVE
practices.body: Jesus prayed for those also who will believe in me through their word, and someone prayed that way for you. Write down three names of men who do not yet believe — a neighbor, a coworker, a son. Pray for each by name every morning this week. Ask the Father to bring them to faith through the word of Christ, and ask Him to put that word in your mouth when the door opens.

practices.title: GO TO THE BROTHER
practices.body: Name the believer you have kept at a distance — the man who wronged you at the business meeting, the brother you stopped calling after the job went sideways. Christ has given you both the same glory. This week, go to him. Do not wait for him to come first. Say what needs saying, forgive what needs forgiving, and shake his hand as a man who shares the same Father.

practices.title: WATCH WHAT YOU SAY ABOUT HIS PEOPLE
practices.body: Count the side comments you make this week about other believers and other churches — at lunch, in the car, at supper in front of your kids. The world is listening for whether Christ’s people love one another. When you must disagree, disagree plainly and hold to the truth, but do not sneer. Speak of His people as people He prayed for, because He did.

practices.title: READ THE APOSTLES’ WORD ALOUD
practices.body: You believed through their word, and that word is how others will believe too. Pick one evening this week and read John 17 aloud at home — with your wife, your kids, or alone if you live alone. Read it slowly. Stop at verse 20 and tell whoever is listening that Jesus prayed there for everyone who would believe, before any of them were born.

practices.title: LOOK AHEAD TO WHERE HE IS
practices.body: When the week goes hard — the work slow, the doctor’s call, the long night with a sick child — read John 17:24 and look past the hard thing. The Son wants you with Him, to see His glory. Let that settle what you fear about the end. Thank Him for it by name before you sleep, and get up the next morning as a man who is wanted.

title: That They May All Be One
subtitle: from dust to the glory He has given
keyVerse: That they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.

passage.text: Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who will believe in me through their word,
that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
The glory which you have given me, I have given to them; that they may be one, even as we are one;
I in them, and you in me, that they may be perfected into one; that the world may know that you sent me and loved them, even as you loved me.
Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am, that they may see my glory, which you have given me, for you loved me before the foundation of the world.
Righteous Father, the world hasn’t known you, but I knew you; and these knew that you sent me.
I made known to them your name, and will make it known; that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

stationsIntro: These are the last lines Jesus prayed before the arrest, and you are in them. Read each verse as a man overhearing the Son speak to His Father about him, then let the Greek word show you what was asked and what was given.
lifeIntro: You were prayed for before you believed. Jesus asked the Father for men who did not yet believe, gave them the glory the Father gave Him, and asked that the Father’s love be in them. None of these practices earns you a place among His people. They are how a man lives once he knows the Son has already put him there.
lifePulls: Jesus did not wait to see how you would turn out before He prayed for you. He asked for your faith, gave you His glory, and told His Father He wants you with Him. Everything you do this week stands on that.
prayer: Father, thank You that Your Son prayed for me before I was born. Thank You for the apostles’ word, by which I came to believe in Him. You have given me the glory You gave Your Son, and made me one with all Your people. Forgive me for the grudges I keep and the side comments I make about those You have joined to me. Teach me to love my brothers, so that the world may believe that You sent Him. Thank You that You love me with the love You have for Your Son. Keep making Your name known to me, through Your word and by Your Spirit. Bring me at last to be with Him where He is, and to see His glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, thank You that Your Son prayed for me before I was born.
Thank You for the apostles’ word, by which I came to believe in Him.
You have given me the glory You gave Your Son, and made me one with all Your
people.
Forgive me for the grudges I keep and the side comments I make about those You
have joined to me.
Teach me to love my brothers, so that the world may believe that You sent Him.
Thank You that You love me with the love You have for Your Son.
Keep making Your name known to me, through Your word and by Your Spirit.
Bring me at last to be with Him where He is, and to see His glory.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Before the arrest, Jesus prayed for you. He asked the Father to make all who believe one, as the Father and the Son are one, and He gave them His glory to make it so. He asked that the world see the Father loves them as He loves the Son. Then He told the Father what He wants: you, with Him, where He is. Stop living like a stranger to His people. You are wanted.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the Son who prayed for you before you had a name. Look to the Son who looked past the eleven and saw you coming. Look to the Son who gave you the glory His Father gave Him and kept none of it back. Look to the Son who, with the soldiers already on their way, spent His last quiet words asking that the Father’s love be in you.

The dust has told you that you are on your own. It has told you the church is a crowd of strangers and God is busy elsewhere. It has told you that if you get in at the end, you will get in by the back door and sit where no one notices. You have believed it on the drive home from church. You have believed it in a hospital hallway. It has kept you on the edge of God’s people for years.

But hear what the Son said to His Father, out loud, the night before He died: Father, I desire that they also whom you have given me be with me where I am. He did not ask the Father to put up with you. He asked to have you. Then He rose from that prayer, crossed the Kidron, and gave Himself up to the torches, so that nothing would stand between you and the place He wants you. He went to the cross for it. He walked out of the grave for it. And at His Father’s right hand He has not stopped asking for you.

So carry His prayer into this week. When you feel alone in the pew, remember you are one with every man who believes, by His gift and not your effort. When a brother has wronged you, remember the same love rests on him. When you lie awake and wonder whether God wants you, remember that the Son told His Father He does. When you stand at a believer’s grave, remember where that man is now: with Christ, where He is, seeing His glory. The Father always hears His Son. He heard Him about you.
closingVerse: That they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.
carry: Jesus prayed that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you; which believer will you stop holding at arm’s length this week, now that you know the Son has made you one with him?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Sooner or later something comes for a man at night. A call from the sheriff’s office. A letter from a lawyer. A son in trouble two counties over. Or the thing you did years ago, found out at last, coming up the drive with its lights on. In that hour a man learns where he stands. You stand in the doorway in your sock feet, and as far as you can tell you are standing alone, with nobody between you and what is coming.

The dust says that is how it always goes. Your sins come home, and when they do, God is nowhere in the yard. You stand in front of your own sin. You take what you have coming. And if there is a God in it, He is a long way off, or He was caught as flat-footed as you were. Read the arrest of Jesus with that voice in your ear and you will see a victim — a good man trapped by a traitor and hauled off by force.

That reading leaves you face-down with no one to lift you, and the dust has you right where it wants you. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) The word that revives a man here is not advice on how to face the torches bravely. It is news that Someone has already faced them for him.

That news is what John 18:1–14 carries. Nobody catches Jesus in this garden. He walks out to meet the men who came for Him, asks them who they are looking for, and gives Himself up on one condition: let these go their way.

sections.heading: Out of the Prayer, Into the Garden
pulls: Nobody caught Jesus in that garden. He walked out to meet the men who came for Him, gave Himself up, and set one condition on the arrest: that His men go free.
paras: The prayer is over. John has just given you the Son’s words to His Father about the men He was given. Now he shows you the Son keeping them with His own body. When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden. John does not tell you what Jesus prayed among the trees. He tells you what Jesus did when the torches came. And what He did, from the first step to the last, was for the men behind Him.

Watch Jesus in every verse of this passage. Judas leads, the soldiers carry weapons, Peter swings a sword, the officers bind Him and march Him to Annas. But none of them runs this night. Jesus asks the questions. Jesus gives the orders. Jesus decides who goes free. John does not even mention the traitor’s kiss that the other Gospels record. In his telling, your eye stays on the Man who steps forward. He is taken because He gives Himself, and He gives Himself so that His men are not taken.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE PLACE JUDAS KNEW
paras: He went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered. Jesus does not go out alone. He takes His men with Him into a place they knew together. And John tells you why that matters: Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.

Jesus knew Judas had gone out into the night. He knew what Judas had gone to do. He could have gone anywhere else in the dark. He went where He always went. He did not change His habits to save His life. He walked to the one spot the traitor was sure to look. The hour His Father had set had come, and He would not slip away from it.

Judas then, having taken a detachment of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons. Soldiers and officers, sent by the rulers, armed and carrying lights — all of it for one Man who had never lifted a hand against anyone. He had healed their sick and fed their hungry. He had taught openly in the temple. Now they come for Him by night, led by a man who had eaten from His hand.

And they bring lanterns to find the One who said, I am the light of the world. Men in the dark, holding up their small flames, hunting for the Light. John told you at the start how that goes: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it. They will lay hands on Him tonight. They will not put Him out.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: WHO ARE YOU LOOKING FOR?
paras: Jesus therefore, knowing all the things that were happening to him, went out. Read the order. He knew everything that was coming — the binding, the trials, the whip, the cross. Knowing it, He went out. He did not wait among the trees to be dragged from cover. He stepped forward and spoke first: Who are you looking for?

They answer, Jesus of Nazareth, and He says, I am he. In the Greek, Jesus says two words: I am. The WEB adds he to make the English plain. But John has been teaching you to hear those two words all through his Gospel: the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd. Jesus said them to the men who hated Him in the temple: before Abraham came into existence, I AM. The One standing in the torchlight answers with the name God gave Moses at the bush.

When therefore he said to them, “I am he,” they went backward, and fell to the ground. John does not explain it, and you do not need him to. Armed men, a crowd with lights, and one word from an unarmed Man puts them on their backs in the dirt. Then He stands there and waits for them to get up.

That is the whole night in one picture. They could not have taken Him if He had not let them. He would tell Pilate so: You would have no power at all against me, unless it were given to you from above. He had said it long before, about His own life: No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. Whatever happens next in this garden, Jesus is not a victim. He is the Good Shepherd, laying down His life.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: LET THESE GO THEIR WAY
pulls: Jesus stepped between the soldiers and His men and turned the arrest onto Himself. That is your salvation in small. He was bound so you could be loosed. He went to judgment so you could go your way.
paras: Again therefore he asked them, “Who are you looking for?” He asks a second time, and this time the question has an edge on it. He makes them say whom they came for: Him, not Peter, not John, not the frightened men behind Him in the dark.

I told you that I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these go their way. The Shepherd steps between the wolves and the sheep. He hands Himself over and sets the terms: take Me, and the eleven walk. And they did walk. Every one of them got out of that garden, and Jesus was bound and led away alone.

John tells you why it went that way: that the word might be fulfilled which he spoke, “Of those whom you have given me, I have lost none.” He had said it in His prayer that same night. He had said it in the synagogue at Capernaum: of all he has given to me I should lose nothing. Now He keeps that word with His own body. Not one of His is lost, because He let Himself be taken.

You know what it is to let another man take the heat — the blame shifted onto a coworker, the silence while someone else carried the write-up for your mistake. Christ did the opposite. The charge was yours, and He turned the arrest onto Himself. He was bound so you could be loosed. He went to judgment so you could go your way. That is not a lesson in courage for you to copy first. It is a rescue for you to receive. When the accuser comes for you this week with your record in his hand, the Shepherd is still standing in front of you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THE CUP THE FATHER HAS GIVEN
paras: Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus. Peter told Jesus at the table, I will lay down my life for you, and here he is, one man with a short blade against a detachment, swinging. You can admire the nerve. But he is fighting the very thing Jesus walked out to meet.

Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it? Jesus does not argue tactics. He names the cup. The prophets spoke of a cup in the Lord’s hand; Isaiah calls it the cup of his wrath. That is the cup Jesus means to drink to the bottom. And because He drinks it, the Lord can say to His people what He said through Isaiah: I have taken out of your hand the cup of staggering.

Notice who gives the cup. Not Judas. Not the chief priests. The Father has given it. The cross was not the plan going wrong. It was the plan. The Father gave the cup, the Son took it willingly, and Peter’s sword could only get in the way.

So the detachment, the commanding officer, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him. The hands through which all things were made are tied with rope. They lead Him to Annas, father-in-law of Caiaphas — the man who had told the council that it was expedient that one man should perish for the people. Caiaphas meant it as cold policy. God meant it as the gospel. One Man did perish for the people, and you are one of the people He perished for.

stations.verse: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.
stations.question: Having prayed for His men to be kept, Jesus went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron to keep them with His own body; where do I need to trust that His care for me goes past words?
stations.gloss: a winter-flowing stream; a torrent
body: Cheimarros is built from the words for winter and for flowing. It names a winter-flowing stream, a torrent. In the Greek Old Testament it mostly stands for the Hebrew nachal. The New Testament has it in one verse, this one.

John names the stream and the garden beyond it. The Son had just finished praying for His men. Now He crossed the water toward the place where He would be taken, and He did not go alone: he went out with his disciples.

The dust says that when trouble comes for you, God stays on the far bank. Cheimarros marks the place where the Son crossed over to meet it. He went into your night ahead of you, and He went on purpose.
stations.live: Name the trouble you have been facing as if you were alone in it. Each morning this week, before you start the day, say: ‘Jesus crossed the Kidron for me. He is already on this side.’

stations.verse: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.
stations.question: Jesus led His men into the garden though Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place; what does it do to the guilt I carry to see that He did not hide from the arrest that saved me?
stations.gloss: a garden
body: Kēpos is the ordinary word for a garden. In the Greek Old Testament it renders the Hebrew gan. It appears in four verses of the New Testament, and three of them are in John’s account of the last night and the burial.

John opens the passion in a garden and closes it in one. Here Jesus is taken. A servant later asks Peter, Didn’t I see you in the garden with him? And when it is over, in the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid. He was arrested among the trees and buried among them, and the grave in that second garden could not keep Him.
The dust says a garden is where a man gets found out and loses everything. In John the garden is where the Son let Himself be found, so that a grave would not be the last word over you.
stations.live: Pick a place this week — the back field, the porch, the shop before anyone else arrives — and meet Christ there each day. Begin with this: ‘You let Yourself be found for me.’

stations.verse: Judas then, having taken a detachment of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons.
stations.question: Judas had walked beside Jesus for years and still came back by night with lanterns, torches, and weapons; what shows that my own faith rests on Christ Himself and not on years spent near Him?
stations.gloss: a torch or lantern
body: Phanos comes from the verb to shine. It means a torch or a lantern, a light a man carries in the dark. The New Testament uses it once, here, where the WEB renders it lanterns. It sits beside torches and weapons — the gear of men sent out to take someone by night.

John has already told you the hour when Judas left the table: It was night. Now he comes back with lights in hand, hunting the One who said, I am the light of the world. A borrowed flame went looking for the Light, and the Light stepped out and spoke first.

The dust says the dark in you is stronger than He is, that one bad night can undo you for good. But a garden full of lanterns could not put Him out, and your dark cannot either. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.
stations.live: When you walk out into the dark this week — the early shift, the late drive home — say it plainly: ‘Christ is the light of the world, and the dark did not put Him out.’

stations.verse: Simon Peter therefore, having a sword, drew it, struck the high priest’s servant, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.
stations.question: Simon Peter swung a sword to stop the arrest Jesus had walked out to meet; where am I fighting with my own hands against something God is doing that I do not yet understand?
stations.gloss: a short sword or dagger; a large knife
body: In older Greek, machaira named a large knife used for sacrifice; the Greek Old Testament uses it for the knife in Abraham’s hand in Genesis 22:6, 10. In the New Testament it is a short sword or dagger. It appears in twenty-six verses, and Paul turns it to the Word: the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Peter’s blade cut off an ear and nothing more. Matthew records what Jesus said next: all those who take the sword will die by the sword. A sword could not save Jesus, and He did not want saving that way. The work in front of Him called for a sacrifice, not a fight.

The dust says you have to win with your own hands — the cutting word, the threat, the temper that clears a room. Christ puts another sword in your hand: the word of God. It does not take off ears. It gives life.
stations.live: Name the sword you reach for when you feel cornered — the sharp tongue, the slammed door, the threat. When your hand goes to it this week, stop and say: ‘Christ did not fight His way out. I will not fight mine.’

stations.verse: Jesus therefore said to Peter, “Put the sword into its sheath. The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it?
stations.question: Jesus told Peter, Put the sword into its sheath, because He meant to drink the cup which the Father has given me; what am I still trying to settle with my own strength that Christ settled when He drank that cup?
stations.gloss: a case or holder; the sheath of a sword
body: Thēkē comes from the verb to put or to place. It means a place where something is put — a chest, a case, a holder. In the New Testament it appears only here, as the sheath of Peter’s sword.

Put the sword into its sheath. Jesus sends the blade back where it belongs, and then says why: The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not surely drink it? The sword goes into its case because the cup is going into His hands. He will drink what Isaiah called the cup of his wrath, so the Lord can tell His people, I have taken out of your hand the cup of staggering.
The dust says you must fight for your own rescue or there will be none. Christ says put it away. He drank the cup to the bottom. There is nothing left in it for you.
stations.live: When guilt over an old sin comes back this week, picture Peter’s blade sliding into its sheath, and say: ‘Christ drank the cup. There is nothing left in it for me.’

practices.title: LET HIM ANSWER THE ACCUSER
practices.body: When the old accusation comes for you this week — the thing you did, the man you were — do not step forward to argue your case. Christ already stepped forward. Remember what He told the soldiers: If therefore you seek me, let these go their way. Then read Romans 8:1 out loud: There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. Let Him stand where you stood.

practices.title: STAND IN FRONT OF YOUR OWN
practices.body: Christ covered His men with His own body. You are called to cover yours, and you do it because He did it first for you. This week, when something goes wrong at home, own your part before anyone asks. At work, do not let another man carry the blame for your mistake. Stand between your wife and the worry, and between your kids and your temper.

practices.title: PUT YOUR SWORD AWAY
practices.body: Name the weapon you reach for when you feel cornered: the cutting word, the threat to quit, the silence that punishes, the lawyer’s number. Jesus told Peter to sheathe the sword because the Father’s plan did not need it. Pick the fight you have been itching to win this week and lay it down. Pray over it instead, and leave the outcome with the Father who gave His Son the cup.

practices.title: KEEP A KNOWN PLACE
practices.body: Jesus often met there with his disciples. He had a place, and He kept it even on the night it cost Him everything. Choose a place and a time to meet Him this week — the porch at first light, the tool bench before the crew shows up, the cab at lunch. Go there every day with John open. Let your family know that is where you go, and why.

practices.title: READ WHAT WAS IN THE CUP
practices.body: One evening this week, read Isaiah 51:17–22 and then John 18:11. See what was in the cup, and see who drank it. Write down the sin you still carry guilt for. Beside it, write the Lord’s promise: I have taken out of your hand the cup of staggering. Then thank Christ by name, out loud, that He did not set the cup down. Do it again the next time that guilt comes knocking.

title: Whom Are You Seeking?
subtitle: from dust to the Shepherd who goes out to meet them
keyVerse: Jesus answered, “I told you that I am he. If therefore you seek me, let these go their way,
