bottomLine: Pilate found no charge against Jesus and had Him flogged anyway. The soldiers crowned Him with thorns and dressed Him in purple for a laugh. Pilate held Him up — Behold, the man — and the priests shouted for the cross and claimed no king but Caesar. None of it slipped out of the Father’s hand. The innocent Man stood under the sentence you earned. Get out of the judge’s chair. Look at Him. He is your King.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and do what Pilate told the crowd to do. Look at the thorns that came up out of your ground. Look at the stripes your sin cut into His back. Look at the hands that made the world, taking the blows without striking back. Look at the governor’s platform and the Judge of all the earth standing below it, silent. Look, and do not look away, because Pilate said it better than he knew: Behold, the man. This is the Man God sent for you.

You have heard the dust say that a king looks like winning. It has told you that a man who is beaten and laughed at has been dropped by God. It has told you that you hold the chair — that you may weigh Jesus and hand down your ruling whenever it suits you. And it has told you that you still have a beating coming, that God is waiting in the back room with the whip. It has kept you face-down for years, guarding a verdict that was never yours to give.

But hear what happened in that courtyard. The whip came down on Him. The curse of the ground was pressed onto His head. The sentence you earned was spoken over Him by a frightened man who had said three times there was no case. And none of it was out of control. Every blow fell inside the Father’s plan, and the Son walked into it with His eyes open. He was not dragged. He was given, and He gave Himself. By his wounds we are healed.

So when the old guilt comes up for review this week, send it to Gabbatha. Look at the Man who stood there in your place, crowned and robed and condemned. When you fear your Caesar, remember where all power comes from. When you are tempted to sit in judgment on His word, get down off the seat and stand where He stood. The King in thorns did not stay in thorns. He went from that courtyard to the cross, and out of the grave on the first day of the week, and He wears a better crown now. He reigns for you. Behold your King.
closingVerse: Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. Pilate said to them, “Behold, the man!
carry: Pilate brought Jesus out in thorns and purple and said Behold, the man; when your guilt rises this week, what will it mean for you to look at Him standing there in your place?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: There is a kind of man who never believes a job is done. He goes back to check the lock. He rereads the email after it is sent. He lies awake going over the bid, the bill, the thing he said at supper. You may be that man. And whatever you do with locks and bids, you almost certainly do it with God.

The dust tells you the account with heaven is still open. It says Christ did His part and now you must do yours, and nobody can tell you when yours is enough. It says the old sin is still on the books — paid down, maybe, but not cleared. So you make payments. A better week. A longer prayer. A promise to yourself in the shower. And the balance never seems to move.

A man buried under a ledger like that does not need a pep talk. He needs a verdict from outside himself, spoken by someone with the right to speak it. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Here is the word. It comes from a cross outside Jerusalem, from a dying Man with breath enough for one more sentence: It is finished.

John does not hand you a technique for quieting a guilty conscience. He hands you a finished work and the Man who finished it. The question this week is not how much more you must do. It is whether you will take Him at His word.

sections.heading: The Hour the Whole Book Was Waiting For
pulls: The dust says your account with God is still open and the payments are yours to make. Jesus bowed His head on a hill near the city and said It is finished. Nothing is left owing.
paras: Everything in John has been leaning toward this afternoon. At Cana Jesus said, My hour has not yet come. John the Baptist pointed and named Him the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. Jesus said the Son of Man must be lifted up as Moses lifted the serpent. He said The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. On the night before, He told His Father, I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do. Now the work is done in the open, on a hill near the city, in the light of day.

The man who wrote this book was there. He is the disciple whom he loved, standing near the cross with the women, and he tells you plainly that he wrote so you would believe. Read the fourteen verses straight through, then read them again slowly. Do not hurry on to the empty tomb. Stand here a while first, near enough to hear Him. Everything your guilt requires was settled on this hill.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: THE PLACE OF A SKULL
paras: He went out, bearing his cross. No one had to drag Him. The One who walked out to meet the soldiers in the garden walks out now carrying the wood they will nail Him to. He goes to a place named for a skull — Golgotha — a place of death and bone and dust. Adam was told, you are dust, and you shall return to dust. The Son of God walked to the very ground where that sentence lives.

Where they crucified him, and with him two others, on either side one, and Jesus in the middle. Isaiah said the Servant would be counted with the transgressors. There He hangs, in the middle, in the worst company the city could find. That is where He chose to be found. If you have ever thought your sin put you too low for Christ to reach, look where He went. He went lower, and He went there on purpose.

Then Pilate writes a sign: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS. It goes up in Hebrew, Latin and Greek, close enough to the city that many of the Jews read this title. The chief priests want it changed so it reads as a claim. Pilate will not move: What I have written, I have written.

Pilate had his own reasons. God had His: the sign was a proclamation. Over the cross, in three tongues, the truth was nailed up for the world to read. The King is not losing His throne on that tree. He is winning His people from the Place of a Skull. Every man who walked past that day could read who was dying there. Every man who reads John still can.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: THE COAT AND THE MOTHER
paras: The soldiers divide His clothes four ways. Then they come to the coat: Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout. They will not tear it, so they throw lots. They are doing what soldiers do at an execution, and they have no idea they are fulfilling a psalm written long before: They parted my garments among them. For my cloak they cast lots. John adds, Therefore the soldiers did these things. Even men with dice in their hands could not step outside what God had written. Stripped and gambled over, Christ was still exactly where Scripture put Him. If God kept His word down to a coat, He will keep His word to you.

Now look at who else is there. But standing by Jesus’ cross were his mother, his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. And the disciple He loved. Jesus, in the middle of bearing the sin of the world, sees His mother. Woman, behold, your son. Then to the disciple: Behold, your mother. From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.

Do not build more on this than John does. A dying Son is making sure His mother will have a home. He honors her with the breath He has left. The Lamb carrying the sin of the world still has room in His heart for one woman standing at the foot of His cross. That is your Savior. He did not love the world in general and forget the people standing in front of Him. Before the supper John wrote that He loved them to the end, and here is the end, and He is still loving His own. If He saw to His mother from the cross, He has not forgotten your house.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: I AM THIRSTY
pulls: He sat by a well and offered living water. On the cross He said I am thirsty, and they lifted vinegar to Him on hyssop. He went dry so that you could drink and never thirst again.
paras: After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, I am thirsty. Watch the order. Jesus knows that all things were now finished. He is not in a fog. Nothing has overtaken Him. He sees that the work is complete, and then He speaks so that one more line of Scripture will be kept.

This is the Man who sat by Jacob’s well about the sixth hour and asked a woman, Give me a drink, then offered her water that would leave her never thirsting again. This is the Man who stood up at the feast and cried, If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. Now the Fountain is dry. The Word through whom every river was made asks for a drink. The psalm had said it: In my thirst, they gave me vinegar to drink. He went dry so you could drink. Every thirst you have tried to quench at the bottom of a glass or in the glow of a screen is a thirst He came to answer with living water.

Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth. John names the plant, and the name carries weight. On the first Passover God told His people to take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood of the lamb and mark their doorposts. Where the blood was, judgment passed over. Now, at Passover, hyssop is lifted to the lips of the Lamb of God. His blood is about to be the mark on your door, and no judgment comes through a door He has marked.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: IT IS FINISHED
paras: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished. John uses the same verb two verses earlier: all things were now finished. It means brought to its end, completed, accomplished. Not I am finished, as if a spent man were giving up. It is finished — the work the Father gave Him. Now He says from the cross what He said in prayer the night before, and it is true to the last line.

What was finished? Everything that stood between you and God. The law you broke, He kept. The punishment you earned fell on Him: Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all. Paul puts it as a debt cancelled. God has forgiven us all our trespasses, wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross. The record against you was not paid down. It was nailed up and taken away. Every priest of old stood day by day at his work. This Priest, when he had offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down on the right hand of God. For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified.

Then John writes, He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit. Death did not take Him. He bowed, and He gave. No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. He laid down His head the way a man sets down his tools when the job is done, and He gave His spirit up to the Father.
So stop making payments. Your penance, your streak, your better months — none of it adds to this. Believe Him. The garden tomb that could not hold Him is the Father’s amen to that cry.

stations.verse: He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”.
stations.question: Jesus went out, bearing his cross, to the Place of a Skull, ground marked by bone and death, and He went willingly; what fear of my own grave am I still carrying as if He had not gone there first?
stations.gloss: a skull
body: Kranion means a skull, and it is related to an old word for the head. Each Gospel uses it once, four verses in all, and every one names the same place: the Skull, where Jesus was crucified. All four writers name it. None of them explains the name.

John gives it in Greek and then in Hebrew — Golgotha. A skull is what is left when the flesh goes back to the ground. Jesus walked there bearing his cross, to the place that looks like the end of every man: bone and dust. He went to death’s own address.

The dust says the skull is where every road ends, and you are walking toward it with nothing in your hands. Christ walked there first, carrying the wood. He died at the Place of a Skull and rose from a tomb near that same ground, so death is not the last stop for the man who belongs to Him.
stations.live: When the thought of your own death comes this week — at a funeral, in a waiting room, on a birthday — say it plainly: ‘He went to the Place of a Skull before me. My grave is not the end of my road.’

stations.verse: Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.
stations.question: Pilate refused to soften the sign into a mere claim, and it stood over the cross: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS; where am I treating Christ’s kingship as His claim rather than as plain fact over my week?
stations.gloss: a title; a written notice
body: Titlos is a word Greek borrowed from Latin. It means a title or an inscription, a written notice put up for people to read. The New Testament has it in two verses only, side by side in John 19.

Pilate wrote it and put it on the cross. John says many read it, because the place was near the city and the words stood in Hebrew, Latin and Greek. The priests wanted it softened into a claim. Pilate refused. The notice nailed over God’s Son told the plain truth, whatever Pilate meant by it.

The dust says Christ’s kingship is a matter of opinion — something He claimed and you may weigh. The sign answers otherwise. It was put up by His enemy, and it stood: What I have written, I have written. God does not revise what He has said about His Son, and the King on that sign is your King.
stations.live: Write the words of that sign on a card and put it where you start work. When you are tempted to bend His rule to suit the day, read it and say: ‘He is King. What God has written stands.’

stations.verse: Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also the coat. Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.
stations.question: Soldiers threw dice for His seamless coat at the foot of the cross, and John says even that fulfilled Scripture; where am I doubting that God is keeping His word because all I can see right now is loss?
stations.gloss: without seam; unsewn
body: Araphos means without a seam. It stands close to the verb to sew, and it describes a garment not sewn together from pieces. It occurs once in the whole New Testament, here at the foot of the cross.

John tells you the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout, and that the soldiers would not tear it. So they cast lots, that the Scripture might be fulfilled. Psalm 22 had said they would cast lots for my clothing. Men with dice at the foot of a cross were keeping God’s word without knowing it.

The dust says your days are loose threads — random, unplanned, coming apart at every seam. Look at the coat. God’s word held right down to a garment and a throw of the dice. A God that careful about His Son’s coat is not careless with your life, and His promises to you are not stitched together from scraps.
stations.live: Find one promise in Scripture you have quietly stopped believing — that He will not leave you, that He will finish what He began. Write it down and read it each morning: ‘He kept His word down to a coat. He will keep this.’

stations.verse: Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth.
stations.question: Jesus, who had offered living water at Jacob’s well, said I am thirsty and was given vinegar on hyssop; what thirst am I still taking to other wells instead of to the One who went dry for me?
stations.gloss: hyssop; a plant used for sprinkling
body: Hyssōpos is hyssop, a plant of which a bunch was used in Israel’s ritual sprinklings. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the Hebrew word for hyssop. Two New Testament verses use it: this one, and one in Hebrews, where Moses sprinkled the book and the people with blood, using water and scarlet wool and hyssop.

At the first Passover God told His people to take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood and mark the doorposts. David prayed, Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. So when John says the vinegar was lifted on hyssop to the dying Lamb at Passover, he is not handing you a gardening note.

The dust wants you to believe you are too stained to be clean. Hyssop never did the cleansing. The blood did. And the blood that makes you clean was poured out by the very Man that branch was lifted to.
stations.live: Pray Psalm 51:7 each night this week over the sin that makes you feel unclean: ‘Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean.’ Then thank Christ by name that His blood is what makes it true.

stations.verse: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.
stations.question: Jesus said It is finished, then bowed his head, and gave up his spirit by His own will; what am I still trying to add to the work He declared complete?
stations.gloss: to bow; to lean or lay down
body: Klinō means to bend or bow, and so to lean or rest. It stands in seven verses of the New Testament. The frightened women at the tomb bowed their faces down to the earth. And Jesus used it of Himself: the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.

John 19:30 puts the same verb with the same word for head: He bowed his head. All His working life the Son of Man had no place to lay His head. On the cross, with the work complete, He laid it down — and only then gave up His spirit.

The dust says a man never gets to lay his head down, because there is always one more thing. Christ bowed His head because there was nothing left to do. He did not drop it in defeat. He laid it down like a man at the end of a finished day, and His rest is yours.
stations.live: Tonight when you lie down, before you run through tomorrow’s list, say John 19:30 aloud and then: ‘He finished it. I can lay my head down too.’

practices.title: ANSWER WITH THREE WORDS
practices.body: Memorize John 19:30. When the accusation comes — over the money you took, the years you were gone, the thing you did at twenty-two — do not argue the facts. You will lose on the facts. Answer with His word: It is finished. Say it out loud in the truck if you have to. The accuser wants a new trial. Christ has already said the work is done, and His word outranks every voice in your head.

practices.title: TEAR UP THE PAYMENT PLAN
practices.body: Make a list of what you do to stay right with God — the extra prayers after a bad night, the penance of feeling rotten long enough, the good deed to balance the scale. Read Hebrews 10:12–14 over the list. Keep the prayers and the good deeds, but take the price tags off them. Do them this week as a son already forgiven, not as a debtor working off a balance. Watch what happens to them when fear is no longer the engine.

practices.title: SEE TO YOUR OWN
practices.body: From the cross Jesus saw His mother and put her in the care of the disciple He loved. He loved His own to the end, and His mother was one of them. Who in your family needs looking after — an aging parent, a sister on her own, a grandson with no father nearby? Call this week. Fix the leaking faucet. Set up the ride to the doctor. Love that is real has an address and a phone number.

practices.title: DRINK FROM HIM
practices.body: Jesus said I am thirsty so that you could drink and never thirst. Name the well you keep going back to — the bottle, the screen, the praise of other men. This week, every time you reach for it, stop and pray: Lord, I am thirsty, and I come to You to drink. Then tell one brother which well you are walking away from, and ask him to pray for you by name.

practices.title: LAY YOUR HEAD DOWN
practices.body: Christ bowed His head when the work was done. Take one evening this week and stop working on purpose — no bids, no inbox, no projects in the garage. Sit on the porch with your wife or your kids, and before bed read John 19:28–30. For a man whose Savior finished the work, rest is not laziness. It is faith, and your family will see it before they hear you explain it.

title: He Bowed His Head
subtitle: from dust to a debt paid in full
keyVerse: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.

passage.text: He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”,
where they crucified him, and with him two others, on either side one, and Jesus in the middle.
Pilate wrote a title also, and put it on the cross. There was written, “JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.”
Therefore many of the Jews read this title, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city; and it was written in Hebrew, in Latin, and in Greek.
The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate, “Don’t write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but, ‘he said, “I am King of the Jews.” ’ ”
Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.”
Then the soldiers, when they had crucified Jesus, took his garments and made four parts, to every soldier a part; and also the coat. Now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout.

Then they said to one another, “Let’s not tear it, but cast lots for it to decide whose it will be,” that the Scripture might be fulfilled, which says, “They parted my garments among them. For my cloak they cast lots.” Therefore the soldiers did these things.
But standing by Jesus’ cross were his mother, his mother’s sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene.
Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother, “Woman, behold, your son!”
Then he said to the disciple, “Behold, your mother!” From that hour, the disciple took her to his own home.
After this, Jesus, seeing that all things were now finished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I am thirsty.”
Now a vessel full of vinegar was set there; so they put a sponge full of the vinegar on hyssop, and held it at his mouth.
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE FINISHED WORK
stationsIntro: Read each verse as a man standing near the cross, close enough to read the sign over His head. Answer plainly, then let the Greek word bring you back to the work He finished there.
lifeIntro: On a hill near Jerusalem the Son of God finished the work of saving His people, and then He bowed His head. There is nothing left for you to complete. What follows is how a man walks once he believes that — not to pay Him back, but because the books are closed and Christ closed them.
lifePulls: Christ did not say I am finished. He said It is finished. The law kept, the curse carried, the record against you nailed to the cross and taken away. Rest in a work He called complete.
prayer: Father, Your Son went out bearing His cross to the Place of a Skull for me. He was counted with the transgressors so that I would be counted righteous in Him. Thank You that He said It is finished, and that nothing is left for me to add. Thank You that the record against me was nailed to the cross and taken out of the way. Forgive me for trying to add to a work He has finished. When I am thirsty, turn me from the old wells to Christ, who went dry for me. Teach me to care for my own as He cared for His mother from the cross. Let me lay my head down tonight in His finished work. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: Jesus carried His cross to the Place of a Skull and was crucified between two men under a sign that told the truth: the King of the Jews. He saw to His mother. He said I am thirsty so Scripture would be fulfilled. Then He said It is finished, bowed His head, and gave up His spirit by His own will. The work is done. Stop paying. Believe Him, and rest.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the hill near the city. See the sign nailed over His head, telling the truth in three tongues. See the soldiers at their dice and the women standing near. See the hyssop lifted to His mouth. And listen, because He is about to speak, and when He speaks, the whole weight of your guilt will be settled in a single word.

The dust has kept your account open for years. It has sent you notices in the night. It has made you a debtor in your own Father’s house. It has told you the old sin is still on the books, that Christ did His part and the rest is yours, that the balance moves only when you sweat. So you have paid and paid — in shame, in promises, in better weeks — and never once heard anyone say the word enough.

Hear Him say it now. It is finished. The work the Father gave Him is done. The law you broke, He kept. The curse you earned, He carried. The handwriting against you He nailed to that same wood and took out of the way. One sacrifice for sins forever. Isaiah saw it long before: he bore the sins of many and made intercession for the transgressors. Then He bowed His head — not because death had won, but because the work was through — and gave up His spirit to the Father. No one took His life from Him. He laid it down for you.

So when the notice comes this week, do not reach for your wallet. Answer with His word. When your thirst drags you toward the old well, remember the Man who went dry so you could drink. When you lie down tonight, lay your head where He laid His, in a finished work. The tomb near that hill could not keep Him, and the Father raised Him to say the work was accepted. And He who said It is finished has said this too: He who comes to me I will in no way throw out. Your door is marked. Judgment has passed over. Come, then, and rest.
closingVerse: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” He bowed his head, and gave up his spirit.
carry: Jesus said It is finished before He bowed His head, and nothing was left undone; where will you stop trying to settle your account with God this week and rest on His word instead?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: A dead man is heavy. If you have ever carried one end of a casket, you know it in your shoulders — the dead weight, the slow steps across wet grass, the hole cut square in the ground. Nobody hurries at a grave. The work is over. All that is left is to lower him down and put the dirt back.

Then the dust starts talking. It says the grave is the one place God does not go — that at the graveside He goes quiet and leaves the men with shovels to finish up. It says that whatever Jesus was, His story ended the way every story ends: a body, a slab, a stone. And it says one more thing, closer to home. It says your faith can stay a private matter. Believe in the dark if you like. Keep it out of sight at work and at the feed store, where it might cost you something.

The dust has every cemetery on earth to point to, and God Himself said it first to Adam: For you are dust, and you shall return to dust. So the soul goes down and lies flat in it. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) This week the reviving word comes from the last place a man would look for it — a dead body on a cross, a soldier’s spear, two disciples who had kept their faith in the dark, and a new tomb in a garden.

Do not hurry past it. John does not. He slows down at the very spot every man wants to look away from, and he tells you as a sworn witness that the Son of God truly died — and that even His death was held in His Father’s hand, down to the bone.

sections.heading: After the Cry from the Cross
pulls: The dust says God goes quiet at the grave. John stood close enough to see the blood and water and wrote it down so you would know the Son of God truly died — and that not one bone of Him slipped from His Father’s hand.
paras: Last week ended with three words: It is finished. Then Jesus bowed his head, and gave up his spirit. No one took His life from Him. He laid it down. This week picks up in the quiet after that cry. The crowd is thinning. The Preparation Day is running out, and a Sabbath is coming that the leaders do not want spoiled.

The disciple whom Jesus loved stood near that cross, and he is the man who wrote this Gospel. Of these hours he says, He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. So read these twelve verses as the word of a man who watched. There are no speeches. Jesus says nothing at all. Everything is done to His body, by soldiers and then by friends, and over all of it stands what God had written beforehand.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: ALREADY DEAD
paras: Look at who is asking. The same leaders who would not step into Pilate’s headquarters at Passover for fear of being defiled now go back to him with a request. It was the Preparation Day, and they did not want bodies left hanging on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a special one). So they asked of Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away. They were careful about the calendar. They had just handed the Son of God over to be crucified.

That is religion without Christ. It keeps the edges neat. It frets about the holy day while the Lamb hangs dead in front of it. You know the pull of that. The prayer said on time while the grudge keeps running. The offering given while the side comment stays sharp. The dust loves a tidy outside, because a tidy outside costs nothing and changes nothing.

Therefore the soldiers came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who was crucified with him. Then they reached the middle cross. When they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they didn’t break his legs.

Already dead. Men came to hurry His death along, and there was nothing left for them to do. He had said it plainly before: No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. He bowed His head and gave up His spirit before any soldier could reach Him. Nothing you bring can hurry that death or finish it. You cannot add one blow to it, and you do not need to. It was done before the soldiers got there.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: BLOOD AND WATER
paras: However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. John does not tell you why the soldier did it. He tells you what he saw. The spear went in, and out came blood and water. The man on the middle cross was not fainting or sleeping or acting. He was dead.

This matters more than most men think. If Jesus did not truly die, then no one truly died in your place, and your sin is still standing where it stood. But He did die. The Word who became flesh, and lived among us had real blood in His veins, and a soldier’s spear let it out. Blood that cleanses and water that washes are old pictures in Scripture, and you may hear an echo of them here. John does not stop to draw them out. His weight falls on something plainer. It happened, and he saw it.

Then he steps out from behind the story for one sentence and puts his hand on the Book. He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. He knows that he tells the truth, that you may believe. This is not a tale that grew in the telling. It is the testimony of a man who stood there, given for one reason — the same reason he wrote the whole Gospel: that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

So the spear that was meant to make sure of a dead convict ends up making sure of your faith. God turned even a soldier’s thrust into His witness. The dust tells you the cross is a picture for Sundays. John tells you it is a death he watched with his own eyes.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: AS THE SCRIPTURE SAID
pulls: The soldiers came to hurry His death and found the work already done. The Father kept every bone, fulfilled every word, and laid His Son in a new tomb. Nothing about that death was out of His hand.
paras: For these things happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled. John names two. The first: A bone of him will not be broken. When God gave Israel the Passover, He said of the lamb, Do not break any of its bones. The psalm says of the righteous man, He protects all of his bones. Not one of them is broken. The soldiers knew none of that. They walked past a dead man’s legs because there was no reason to break them. But the Father was keeping His Lamb whole. Jesus died at Passover as the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world, and God marked Him out to the last bone.

The second: They will look on him whom they pierced. Read where it comes from. In Zechariah the Lord Himself is speaking: I will pour on David’s house, and on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the spirit of grace and of supplication; and they will look to me whom they have pierced. The One who says me is the Lord. John sets those words under the cross of Jesus. The pierced One is God come in the flesh.

And the look Zechariah describes is not idle. God pours out grace first, and then men look, and they shall mourn for him, as one mourns for his only son. That is how repentance comes — not by whipping yourself up, but by grace that turns your eyes to the One your sin pierced. Revelation says a day is coming when every eye will see him, including those who pierced him. Every man will look at Him one day. Look now, while it is the day of grace, and the look will save you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: A NEW TOMB IN A GARDEN
paras: After these things, Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked of Pilate that he might take away Jesus’ body. John has told you about men like him before: even many of the rulers believed in him, but because of the Pharisees they didn’t confess it. Joseph was one of the quiet ones. John does not tell you what changed in him. He tells you what he did. He walked up to the governor and asked for the body of a crucified man.

Nicodemus, who at first came to Jesus by night, also came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred Roman pounds. This is the man who heard Jesus say, that first night, even so must the Son of Man be lifted up. Now he carries the body that was lifted up. Two disciples who had kept to the dark come out at the burial, in daylight, with their hands full.

So they took Jesus’ body, and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as the custom of the Jews is to bury. Then John marks the place: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid. Jesus was taken in a garden across the Kidron. Now He is laid in one. They laid Jesus there.

Stand at that stone for a moment. The Son of God went all the way down. The psalm said it ahead of time: You have brought me into the dust of death. He did not stop short of the grave. He went where you are going, so that you would never find the grave a place without Him. And a new tomb, never used, was ready in a garden — a place no death had ever owned.

stations.verse: Therefore the Jews, because it was the Preparation Day, so that the bodies wouldn’t remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a special one), asked of Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away.
stations.question: The men who had handed Jesus over to be crucified still fretted that bodies might hang on the cross on the Sabbath; where do I guard the outward habits of my faith while keeping the crucified Christ Himself at arm’s length?
stations.gloss: to break
body: Katagnymi means to break. The New Testament uses it in only four verses. Three of them sit side by side in John 19:31–33: the leaders ask for the legs to be broken, the soldiers break them, and at Jesus they stop.

The fourth is in Matthew, where he quotes the prophet about God’s chosen Servant: He won’t break a bruised reed. The Christ who would not break a bruised man was not broken the way men planned. He had already given up His spirit.

The dust tells you faith is about keeping the edges clean. Those men kept their Sabbath and broke what they could. Christ kept His Father’s word and broke no bruised reed. He will not break you either. He was pierced for you instead.
stations.live: Pick one religious habit you keep mostly for how it looks. Do it this week with the cross in view, and before you start, say: ‘Christ was already dead for me before I lifted a finger.’

stations.verse: However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
stations.question: A soldier drove a spear into the side of a man already dead, and blood and water came out; how would I carry my guilt differently if I took seriously that Jesus truly died in my place?
stations.gloss: a spear; a lance
body: Lonchē names a spear — first the head of it, then the whole weapon, a lance. This is the only verse in the New Testament where it stands.

The spear did what spears do. It went in, and it made certain. Whatever the soldier meant by it, John wants you to see the result: immediately blood and water came out. No one walked away from that place unsure whether the man in the middle had died. The death in your place was not a swoon or a show. It was a death, and it cost Him everything.

The dust likes a softer cross — a Jesus who suffered a while and slipped out the back, a sacrifice that cost something but not all. That cross cannot save you, because it never paid. The spear shuts that door. He died. The payment was real, so the pardon is real.
stations.live: When guilt comes back this week with an old charge, open to John 19:34 and read it aloud. Then say: ‘He truly died. The debt was paid by a real death, and my pardon is as real as His blood.’

stations.verse: However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
stations.question: John stood close enough to see blood and water come from Jesus’ side, and he swore to it that you may believe; what doubt about Christ’s death for me do I need to bring under that eyewitness word?
stations.gloss: the side of the body
body: Pleura means the side, the flank of a body. Five New Testament verses use it. One is in Acts, where an angel strikes Peter on the side. The other four are John’s, and every one of them names the side of Jesus.

Here the spear opens it. On the evening He rose, the Lord showed them his hands and his side. Eight days later He tells Thomas, Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. The wound John saw opened on the cross is the wound the risen Christ holds out to frightened men. The side is the proof that the One who lives is the One who died.
The dust says the cross is a symbol, a shape on a steeple. John says it is a side he watched opened. When you doubt, look there. The wound He kept is evidence you can stand on.
stations.live: Read John 19:34–35 and 20:19–20 together one evening this week. Write one line beneath them: ‘The One who rose is the One who was pierced, and He was pierced for me.’

stations.verse: For these things happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled, “A bone of him will not be broken.
stations.question: John says the soldiers passing over His legs fulfilled A bone of him will not be broken, a word first given about the Passover lamb; where am I sheltering under something besides the blood of that Lamb?
stations.gloss: a bone
body: Osteon is a bone. John uses a shortened form of it, inside an Old Testament quotation. The word stands in four verses of the New Testament: whitened tombs full of dead men’s bones, Joseph giving orders about his own bones, the risen Christ’s flesh and bones, and here.

God told Israel of the Passover lamb, Do not break any of its bones. The psalm says of the righteous man, Not one of them is broken. The soldiers knew neither word. But the Father was keeping His Lamb whole and showing you whose blood marks the door.

In Luke the risen Jesus says, a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones, as you see that I have. The bones the soldiers passed over walked out of the tomb. The dust says your bones end in the ground. The Lamb’s unbroken bones say otherwise. He rose in the body, and so will you.
stations.live: Name the thing you lean on when you want to feel right with God — your record, your church, your effort. Set it down in prayer and say: ‘The Lamb’s blood is my only cover.’

stations.verse: Again another Scripture says, “They will look on him whom they pierced.
stations.question: John quotes They will look on him whom they pierced, and in Zechariah that look comes only after God pours out the spirit of grace; whose sin do I actually see when I look at the pierced Christ?
stations.gloss: to pierce; to run through
body: Ekkenteō means to pierce. Only two verses of the New Testament use it. Here John sets Zechariah’s word under the cross. In Revelation the same word looks ahead to Christ’s return: every eye will see him, including those who pierced him.

In Zechariah the Lord Himself speaks: they will look to me whom they have pierced. And the look comes with a gift. God pours out the spirit of grace and of supplication, and men mourn as one mourns for his only son. The piercing was sin. The looking is grace.

The dust tells you to look away from the cross because it shames you. But there is only one look that saves, and it is this one — a look at the Man your sin pierced, who pours out grace on the very ones who pierced Him. Every eye will see Him one day. Look now, while He gives the grace to look.
stations.live: Set aside ten quiet minutes one night. Read Zechariah 12:10 and John 19:37. Name the sins that pierced Him, plainly, and then say: ‘You were pierced for these. I look to You.’

practices.title: READ IT AS TESTIMONY
practices.body: Read John 19:31–42 aloud three times this week, once a day, the way you would read a sworn statement. Stop each time at verse 35: He who has seen has testified, and his testimony is true. John was there. Let that settle on you. When you finish, say one sentence out loud before you close the book: He truly died, and it was for me. Then go to work on that.

practices.title: LOOK AT THE PIERCED ONE
practices.body: Give one evening ten minutes with no phone in reach. Read Zechariah 12:10, John 19:37 and Isaiah 53:5. Name your sins plainly — the money, the anger at your wife, the second drink, the thing on the screen. Do not dress them up. Then read it again: he was pierced for our transgressions. Mourn the sin, and then take the grace. That is the order Zechariah gives: grace poured out, then the look.

practices.title: STEP OUT OF THE DARK
practices.body: Joseph had kept his faith secret for fear of the Jews. Name one place where you have done the same — the crew, the family table, the men you hunt with. This week say one plain sentence about Christ there. Not a sermon. Just the truth: He died for me, and I belong to Him. The One who was not ashamed to die for you will not leave you alone when you say His name.

practices.title: STAND AT A GRAVE WITH HOPE
practices.body: Go to the grave of someone you have buried, or sit with a man who is grieving. Read John 19:41–42 there. The Son of God was laid in a tomb in a garden. He went into the dust of death ahead of you and ahead of the one you lost in Christ. Do not rush past the grief. But name the hope out loud: the grave is a place He has been.

practices.title: STOP ADDING TO A FINISHED DEATH
practices.body: The soldiers came to finish Him off and found Him already dead. When guilt tells you this week that you must pay something more — another promise, another round of beating yourself up — answer it with Hebrews 10:14: For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified. Write that verse where you will see it every morning, and let it do its work.

subtitle: from dust to the body laid in a new tomb

stationsIntro: Read these verses the way John wrote them — as a witness who stood close enough to see. Answer plainly, and let each Greek word bring you back to a death that was real, foretold, and finished for you.
lifeIntro: God kept His Son whole on the cross, fulfilled His word to the letter, and brought two hidden disciples out into the open to bury Him. The death that paid for you was real, foretold, and witnessed. These practices rest on that finished death. None of them adds a thing to it.
lifePulls: Jesus did not slip out of death by a side door. He died, and a soldier’s spear made sure of it. Two secret disciples laid Him in a new tomb, and every word God had spoken over His body held.
prayer: Father, Your Son truly died, and You kept every word You had spoken over Him. Thank You that not one of His bones was broken, and that He is the Lamb whose blood covers me. Thank You that John saw the blood and water and wrote it down so I would believe. Forgive me for keeping the outside of my faith tidy while my heart keeps its distance. Forgive me for the times I have kept quiet about Your Son out of fear. Pour out Your spirit of grace on me, so that I look on the One I pierced and trust Him. Make me as open with His name as Joseph and Nicodemus were at His tomb. When I stand at a grave, remind me that Your Son lay in one before me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
