bottomLine: Jesus was already dead when the soldiers came to break His legs. A spear made it certain, and John saw the blood and water and swore to it so you would believe. Not one bone was broken, because He is the Passover Lamb, and the pierced One is the Lord Zechariah spoke of. Two secret disciples laid Him in a new tomb in a garden. His death was real, foretold, and finished. Stop adding to it. Believe.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the body on the middle cross. Look at the legs the soldiers did not break. Look at the side the spear opened. Look at the blood and water a witness saw and would not keep to himself. Look at the hands of two men who had kept their faith in the dark, now winding linen and spice around the body of their Lord where anyone could see them do it.

The dust has told you the grave is the place God does not go. It has pointed you to every slab and every stone, and to the dirt they shovel back in. It has told you to keep your faith quiet and your head down, to tidy the outside and leave the heart alone. It has told you the last word over every man is dust, and that Jesus got the same last word as everyone else.

But the Son of God went down into the very place the dust brags about. You have brought me into the dust of death. He did not go there by accident or by force. He bowed His head and gave up His spirit, and the soldiers found the work done. His Father kept every bone of Him. His Father kept every word about Him. And His Father had a new tomb waiting in a garden, a tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid, because this was no ordinary burial, and this body would not stay. So carry this into Tuesday. The death that paid for your sin was real. A soldier made sure of it, and an eyewitness swore to it. Nothing you do this week can add to it, and nothing that comes against you can undo it. When your own day comes and they lay you in the ground, you will not be the first to lie there under God’s hand. The Lamb whose bones were kept whole has gone ahead of you. The new tomb in the garden held Him only until the first day of the week, and the One who lay in it will raise you up at the last day.
closingVerse: However one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out.
carry: John watched the spear open Jesus’ side and wrote down the blood and water so that you would believe; what guilt will you set down this week because the death in your place was real and finished?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: Grief gets up early. It wakes you before the alarm, before the coffee, before the birds, and sends you somewhere — the cemetery gate, the hospital lot, the empty side of the bed, the back shed where his tools still hang on their nails. You go because you do not know where else to go. You go to tend what is left.

The dust meets you there with its oldest claim. Dead is dead. The grave keeps what it gets. The best a man can hope for is a decent stone and a few people who remember his name for a while. Love, the dust says, stops at the graveside, and the most you can do for the dead is look after the body. Then it adds one more thing. God does not know your name. You are one of billions, and your tears are just weather.

Mary Magdalene went to the tomb with all of that pressing on her. She had stood by the cross and watched Him die. All she had left was a body, and she went looking for it in the dark. That is what a soul does when it has no word from God. It holds on to what the grave has left. My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV)
On the first day of the week the reviving word came out of a garden. It did not come as an argument or a vision. It came from the mouth of a living Man, and it was one word long. It was her name.

sections.heading: The First Day of the Week
pulls: Grief went to the garden to tend a body. The dust says the grave keeps what it gets. But the stone was already moved, the linen lay empty, and the Lord was standing behind her, ready to say her name.
paras: Jesus was laid in the new tomb on the Preparation Day. The Sabbath came and went. Now it is the first day of the week, and it is still dark. The disciples are scattered, as Jesus said they would be. Peter has denied Him three times by a fire in a courtyard. The women and the disciple whom Jesus loved stood near the cross, and now one of those women walks back toward the garden before sunup.

Do not read this chapter as a rumor that grew. The writer was in it. He ran to the tomb, stooped at the door, and went in, and he tells you what lay inside. Read slowly, and watch three people come to the empty tomb with three kinds of sight — one who looks in, one who goes in, and one who weeps until she is called. By the end of the chapter all three know the same thing. The Lord is alive.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: WHILE IT WAS STILL DARK
paras: Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb. John does not tell you what she planned to do there. He tells you that she went, and when. The dark is not only on the road. She has watched Him die. As far as she knows, she is walking to the last place on earth where He can be found.

She saw the stone taken away from the tomb. She does not go in. She runs to Peter and the other disciple: They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him. Her first explanation is the one the dust would give. Someone has been at the grave. Someone has moved the body. Even the dead are not left alone.

Watch how far grief can see in the dark. Not far. It sees a stone moved and fills in the rest with the worst. You know how that goes — a call that is not returned, a test result that has not come back, and your mind runs straight to the bottom of the hole. Mary was wrong. She was wrong in the best direction a person can be wrong.

Notice how often John uses those words, taken away. The leaders asked that the bodies might be taken away. Joseph took away his body. Now the stone is taken away, and Mary fears the Lord has been too. Long before, the Baptist pointed at Jesus as the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world. That is the taking away that matters this morning, and Mary does not know it yet. The grave has not lost a body. Death has lost its prisoner.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: HE SAW AND BELIEVED
paras: They both ran together. The other disciple outran Peter, and came to the tomb first. He gets there first and stops at the door. Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he didn’t enter in.

Then Peter comes. The man who denied Him three times by a fire comes running, and he does not stop at the door. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered into the tomb. He sees what the other disciple saw: He saw the linen cloths lying. Then he sees the thing that stops a man cold — the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself.

Think about what that means. A man who carries off a body does not unwrap it first and leave the wrappings behind. He does not stop to roll up the head cloth and set it to one side. The cloths are still there, and the body is gone. That is not what a thief leaves behind.

So then the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed. Then John adds a line against himself and his friends: For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Jesus had said it in their hearing: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. The psalm had said it long before: neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption. They were slow, like you. But the tomb did not wait for them to catch up. He was raised whether they understood it yet or not. Then the disciples went away again to their own homes.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: CALLED BY NAME
pulls: He did not walk out of the grave to speak to mankind in general. On the morning He broke death, He stopped beside one weeping woman, and the word that opened her eyes was her name.
paras: But Mary was standing outside at the tomb weeping. The men go home. She stays. So as she wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb. There she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet. They ask her a plain question: Woman, why are you weeping? Her answer has not changed since the dark. They have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.

When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, and didn’t know that it was Jesus. He asks the angels’ question, and then one more: Who are you looking for? He asked the same thing once before, in another garden, of men who came with torches to arrest Him. Now He asks a woman who came to find His body. She takes Him for the gardener. If he has moved the body, she says, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.

Then He says one word. Her name. She turned and said to him, Rabboni — which John tells you means Teacher. She knew Him by His voice before she knew Him by His face. This is what He said the Good Shepherd does: He calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out. And the sheep listen to his voice.

The dust told you that you are one of billions, that God deals in crowds and your tears are weather. On the morning He broke death, the risen Christ stopped for one weeping woman, and the word that opened her eyes was her name. He knows yours. I have called you by your name. You are mine. He came out of the grave calling His own.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: MY FATHER AND YOUR FATHER
paras: Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father. Mary has Him back, and she takes hold of Him. But Jesus is not going back to the old days on the roads of Galilee. He is going up to His Father, and from there He will send the Counselor, as He promised the night before He died. Mary does not need to hold Him in place. He is sending her.

He gives her a message: go to my brothers and tell them. My brothers. Until now in this Gospel He has never called His disciples that. These are the men who scattered and denied Him. He names them brothers on the first morning they could have been named traitors. And the message is this: I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.

Mark the order of it. He does not fold Himself in with them as if He and they stood on the same footing. He is the Son by nature, the one and only Son of the Father. They are made sons through Him. Because He died and rose, His Father is now their Father. As many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children. That is adoption. The Father of Jesus is your Father. The God of Jesus is your God.

Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her. In John’s account the first witness to the risen Lord is a weeping woman with a message to carry. She went from the grave to the brothers with news no grave could keep down. She had seen the Lord. That is still the news, and it still travels one house at a time.

stations.verse: Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he didn’t enter in.
stations.question: The other disciple stooped at the tomb, saw the linen cloths lying, and still stayed outside; what keeps me standing at the doorway of the resurrection, interested but not yet resting my life on it?
stations.gloss: to stoop to look; to look into
body: Parakyptō means to stoop, and then to stoop to look — to bend down and peer in. Five New Testament verses use it. Luke uses it of Peter at the tomb. John uses it twice: of the other disciple here, and of Mary a few verses later.

It can also mean a closer look. James uses it of the man who looks into the perfect law of freedom. Peter uses it of the good news, which things angels desire to look into. The angels lean in to see what you are invited to see. The disciple at the door stayed outside for a moment. Then he went in, and he saw and believed.
The dust is content to let you look from the doorway for a lifetime — interested, respectful, never coming in. But the stone is moved, and the tomb is open. Stoop, look, and then go in.
stations.live: Read John 20:1–10 slowly one morning this week. Write one sentence about what was in that tomb and what was not. Then pray: ‘Lord, I will not stay at the door. I believe You rose.’

stations.verse: Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he didn’t enter in.
stations.question: The linen cloths Joseph and Nicodemus had wound around His body lay in the tomb with no body in them; what does that empty linen say to me about the grave I will one day be laid in?
stations.gloss: a linen cloth; a piece of fine linen
body: Othonion is a piece of fine linen, a linen cloth. It is a small form of the word othonē, and its five New Testament verses all belong to the burial of Jesus and His empty tomb.

John keeps track of the cloths. Joseph and Nicodemus bound it in linen cloths with the spices. On the first day of the week the other disciple stooped and saw the linen cloths lying. The cloths had not moved. The body had. No one carried Him off and left His wrappings neat behind Him.

The dust says the wrappings are the last word: a man goes into the cloth, and the cloth goes into the ground. But the linen lay there like work clothes a man has stepped out of at the end of a shift. Death dressed Him for the grave. He left its clothes behind. One day, in Christ, so will you.
stations.live: Next time you pass a cemetery this week, slow down and say it out loud: ‘The linen lay empty. My Lord left His grave clothes behind, and He will call me out of mine.’

stations.verse: And the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself.
stations.question: The head cloth lay rolled up by itself, and the other disciple saw and believed before he understood the Scripture; what evidence of Christ’s rising do I keep explaining away rather than believing?
stations.gloss: a cloth, a kerchief; a covering for the head of the dead
body: Soudarion came into Greek from Latin. It means a handkerchief — the cloth a servant wrapped his master’s money in, the cloths carried from Paul to the sick. John uses it for the cloth laid over the head of the dead. It stands in four verses.

John’s two uses belong together. At Bethany Lazarus came out bound hand and foot with wrappings, and his face was wrapped around with a cloth. He came out still wearing death, and others had to free him. Here the head cloth is rolled up in a place by itself. No one had to free Jesus.

The dust says your dead stay wrapped. Lazarus was raised to die again. Christ was raised never to die again: Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more. That rolled-up cloth marks a death that is over for good, and a Lord who will call you out too.
stations.live: Write down the one doubt about the resurrection you keep turning over. Read John 20:6–8 beside it. Then answer it in prayer: ‘He left the cloth behind. He is not dead. I believe.’

stations.verse: Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?” She, supposing him to be the gardener, said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.
stations.question: Jesus asked Mary, Who are you looking for?, and because she had come for a body, she took Him for the gardener; in my grief, what smaller thing am I looking for than the living Christ standing near?
stations.gloss: a gardener; the keeper of a garden
body: Kēpouros is a gardener. It is built from kēpos, garden, and a word for one who watches — the garden’s keeper. The New Testament uses it once, in John’s note on what Mary supposed.

John has set these chapters in gardens. Jesus was taken in a garden. He was buried in a garden near the cross. Now He stands there alive, and Mary takes Him for the man who tends it. She is wrong about who He is, but not far wrong about where He belongs. The first man was put in a garden to keep it, and lost it. On the first day of a new week the second Man walks out of a tomb into a garden death cannot keep.
The dust tells you that your grief sees clearly. Mary’s eyes were full, and she looked at Life and saw a groundskeeper. He spoke, and she knew Him.
stations.live: Name the loss that has your eyes full this season. Each morning this week, read John 20:14–16 and pray: ‘Lord, You are not among the dead. Speak, and let me know You.’

stations.verse: Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’
stations.question: Jesus sent word to men who had scattered and denied Him, calling them my brothers and naming His Father as theirs; how will I come to God differently this week if His Father is truly my Father?
stations.gloss: to go up; to ascend
body: Anabainō means to go up. It is an everyday word: a man goes up to Jerusalem or up a tree. Seventy-seven New Testament verses use it.

John gives it a weight all its own. No one has ascended into heaven but he who descended out of heaven, the Son of Man. Jesus asked men who stumbled at His words, what if you would see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? Now, outside the tomb, He says it plainly: I am ascending to my Father and your Father. The One who came down into the dust is going back up, and not as a stranger to you.
The dust says God is far above and you are far below, with a ceiling between. Christ went down to the grave and up to the Father, and He tells you whose Father that is. Yours.
stations.live: Begin every prayer this week with the words He gave Mary: ‘Father, You are His Father and my Father, His God and my God.’ Then talk to Him as a son talks to his father.

practices.title: GO TO THE TOMB EARLY
practices.body: One morning this week, get up before the house does and read John 20:1–18 aloud while it is still dark. Read it as an account, not a mood, and let the dark outside the window remind you where Mary started. Write down what Mary saw, what the other disciple saw, and what Peter saw. Then write what none of them could find. Close the book with one sentence spoken out loud: He is not there. He is risen.

practices.title: SAY IT PLAINLY
practices.body: Mary went straight to the disciples and told them she had seen the Lord. Pick one man this week — a friend, a son, the man on the next machine — and tell him plainly that you believe Jesus rose from the dead in His body. You do not have to win an argument. Tell him what John saw in that tomb, and that you are staking your life on it.

practices.title: TAKE YOUR GRIEF TO THE GARDEN
practices.body: Name the loss you have been carrying. Read John 20:11–16 slowly, and do not hide your tears from God. The risen Christ did not scold Mary for weeping. He asked her, Who are you looking for? Answer Him in your own words. Then wait on the One who stood beside her and spoke her name. He has not gone silent. He still stands near you in His word.

practices.title: ANSWER TO YOUR NAME
practices.body: Write your own name on a card, and under it Isaiah 43:1: I have called you by your name. You are mine. Keep it in your wallet or your lunch pail. When the dust tells you that you are a number to God, take the card out and read it. The Shepherd calls his own sheep by name. He called Mary by hers in a garden, and He has called you.

practices.title: PRAY AS A BROTHER
practices.body: Jesus called men who had failed Him my brothers. Think of one believing man you have written off for what he did. Pray for him by name every day this week, and then call him. Do not open with his failure. Open with what Christ has done for you both: the same Father, the same risen Brother, the same morning. Let grace go first.

title: I Have Seen the Lord
subtitle: from dust to the garden morning
keyVerse: Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.

passage.text: Now on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene went early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw the stone taken away from the tomb.
Therefore she ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we don’t know where they have laid him!”
Therefore Peter and the other disciple went out, and they went toward the tomb.
They both ran together. The other disciple outran Peter, and came to the tomb first.
Stooping and looking in, he saw the linen cloths lying, yet he didn’t enter in.
Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying,
and the cloth that had been on his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but rolled up in a place by itself.
So then the other disciple who came first to the tomb also entered in, and he saw and believed.
For as yet they didn’t know the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead.
So the disciples went away again to their own homes.
But Mary was standing outside at the tomb weeping. So as she wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb,
and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.
They asked her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.”
When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, and didn’t know that it was Jesus.

Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?” She, supposing him to be the gardener, said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”
Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him, “Rabboni!” which is to say, “Teacher!”
Jesus said to her, “Don’t hold me, for I haven’t yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brothers and tell them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ ”
Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.

stationsLabel: THE WORD ON THE EMPTY TOMB
stationsIntro: Read these verses at the pace of someone walking into a garden before sunup. Answer plainly, and let each Greek word bring you to the door of the tomb, looking in at what is no longer there.
lifeIntro: On the first day of the week Christ walked out of the grave, left death’s cloths behind, and called Mary by name. Then He made His Father the Father of His brothers. These practices are the life of a man who has heard that news. They do not win you a place in the family. The place was given on that morning.
lifePulls: The stone was moved, the linen lay empty, and the head cloth was rolled up by itself. The risen Christ called a weeping woman by name and sent her to His brothers with news of His Father and theirs.
prayer: Father, on the first day of the week You raised Your Son from the dead. Thank You that the stone was moved and the grave cloths lay empty. Thank You that Jesus called Mary by name, and that He knows mine. Forgive me for looking for Him among the dead, and for letting grief tell me He is gone. Forgive me for standing at the door of the tomb when You have opened it for me to see. Thank You that His Father is my Father, and His God is my God, because He calls me His brother. Give me Mary’s plain words this week, to tell someone that the Lord is risen. Keep me sure that the grave will not keep me, because it could not keep Him. In Jesus’ name, amen.
prayerLines: Father, on the first day of the week You raised Your Son from the dead.
Thank You that the stone was moved and the grave cloths lay empty.
Thank You that Jesus called Mary by name, and that He knows mine.
Forgive me for looking for Him among the dead, and for letting grief tell me He
is gone.
Forgive me for standing at the door of the tomb when You have opened it for me
to see.
Thank You that His Father is my Father, and His God is my God, because He
calls me His brother.
Give me Mary’s plain words this week, to tell someone that the Lord is risen.
Keep me sure that the grave will not keep me, because it could not keep Him.
In Jesus’ name, amen.
bottomLine: Mary came to the tomb in the dark and found the stone moved. Two disciples ran. One stooped and looked; Peter went in; the other went in after him, saw the cloths lying and the head cloth rolled up, and believed. Then the risen Jesus called Mary by name and sent her to His brothers: His Father is their Father. The grave did not keep Him, and it will not keep you. Go and say so.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to a garden on the first day of the week. See the stone that is no longer where they set it. See the linen lying where a body used to be. See the cloth from His head rolled up in a place by itself, left behind by a Man who has no more use for it. See a woman turn at the sound of her own name, and see her grief give way to the plainest joy a person can know: the one she buried is standing in front of her, alive.

The dust has told you the grave keeps what it gets. It has told you love ends at the graveside, and that the best you can do is tend a stone. It has told you God deals in crowds and does not know your name, and that your tears fall where no one sees. It has told you that a man who scattered and denied can expect a cold welcome, if any welcome at all, and that the best he can hope for is to be kept on the edge of things.

But look where John puts the risen Lord’s first words. Not before Pilate. Not in the temple courts. In a garden, beside one weeping woman, saying Mary. Then He sent her with a message for the men who had failed Him, and He called them my brothers. The One who went down into the dust of death came up out of it with your name in His mouth and His Father’s house open to you.

So take this into your week. When the dust tells you the grave is the end, remember the linen lying empty. When it tells you God does not know you, remember that He said Mary, and that He calls his own sheep by name. When it tells you that you have failed too badly to be family, hear Him say my brothers. He has gone up to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God. His Father is yours. His God is yours. And because He walked out of that tomb in His own body, you will walk out of yours.
closingVerse: Mary Magdalene came and told the disciples that she had seen the Lord, and that he had said these things to her.
carry: Mary went from the empty tomb to the disciples and told them that she had seen the Lord; who will hear from you this week that Jesus is alive and that His Father has become yours?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust has a theory about faith. It says faith belonged to the men who were there. Put you in that room on the first day of the week, let you see His hands, and you would never doubt again. But you were not there. You were born a long way down the road, into a world of feed bills and night shifts, and all you have is a book, a pew, and a handful of men who say they believe. So the dust calls your faith second-hand — a story passed down, good enough for your grandmother, thin as paper next to what Peter and John had.

Then it presses harder. If you have doubts, it says, you must not belong. Real believers do not lie awake wondering whether any of it is true. Real believers do not stand at a graveside and feel the ground go soft under them. The dust takes your questions and turns them into a verdict: you are on the outside, and you will stay there until God shows you something He has not shown you yet.

Some mornings that verdict lands so hard you have no argument left, only an old prayer: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) Look at what the prayer asks for. Not a vision. Not a sign in the sky. A word.

That is what John 20 hands you. A doubting man is met by the risen Christ, sees the wounds, and calls Him God. Then Jesus looks past Thomas, down the years, and speaks a blessing over the man who would never see what Thomas saw. Then John stops and tells you why he wrote the whole book. He wrote it for you.

sections.heading: The Evening of the First Day
pulls: The dust says real faith belonged to the men who saw Him. Jesus calls the man who has not seen and still believes blessed — and John wrote his whole Gospel to put that man in the room.
paras: This same day began in a garden, where Mary Magdalene heard her name and ran to tell the disciples she had seen the Lord. By evening the news had reached the men, and they were still behind shut doors. Jesus comes to them twice in this passage, eight days apart. Both times the doors are locked. Both times His first word is peace.

Between those two visits stands Thomas — the man who once told the others, Let’s go also, that we may die with him, and who asked at the supper, How can we know the way? He missed the first meeting, and he would not take the others’ word for it. The passage closes with John’s own statement of purpose, the sentence that gives this whole four-volume series its name. Read 20:19–31 straight through, and listen for the word believe.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: PEACE BEHIND LOCKED DOORS
paras: When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews. John gives you the hour, the place and the reason. The tomb had been empty since dawn. Mary had told them she had seen Him. And the men who would carry His name to the nations spent the evening with the bolt thrown, listening for footsteps outside. John does not dress them up as brave men. They were afraid, and fear had them shut in.

Then Jesus came and stood in the middle. No knock. No word on how He passed a shut door. He was simply there, among them, in the body that had been laid in the tomb. And His first word asked nothing about where they had been on Friday. He said, Peace be to you.

When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. He did not show them a light or a vision. He showed them wounds. The peace He speaks is not a mood. It is backed by marks in His flesh. The nails and the spear had done their work, and the work had been enough. That is why He can say peace to men who scattered. Their sin had been carried to the cross, and here stood the proof, breathing.

The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord. Fear does not leave a room because men talk themselves out of it. It leaves when the Lord walks in. Whatever has you bolted in this week — the test results, the layoff notice, the thing you did that could still come out — He comes through that door too, and His first word to you is the same.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: AS THE FATHER HAS SENT ME
paras: Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you. He says peace a second time, and this time it is peace for the road. He does not leave them in the room. The Father sent the Son into the world. Now the Son sends these same frightened men out into it, carrying His word.

Then he breathed on them, and said, Receive the Holy Spirit. In the beginning God formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed life into him. Here the risen Son breathes on dust-men again and gives them the Spirit He promised at the supper — the Counselor who would remind you of all that I said to you. They are not sent out on their own breath. Nothing in the mission rests on their nerve, which you have just watched run dry.

If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained. Read it carefully. Jesus does not hand His men a private power to pardon whomever they please. He hands them the gospel. When His apostles and His church declare that every man who believes in Christ is forgiven, they speak what heaven has already settled — mark the words they have been forgiven. When they warn that the man who refuses Him stays in his sins, that word stands too. The authority sits in the message, not in the messenger. Any man who announces Christ crucified and risen carries it, and no man carries it apart from that word.
So the order holds. First His peace, then His wounds, then His Spirit, then His sending. He gives everything before He asks anything.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: MY LORD AND MY GOD
pulls: Thomas set his terms, and Jesus met them with His own wounds. Then He blessed the man who would never see those wounds and would believe anyway. That blessing has your name on it.
paras: But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came. The others found him and told him, We have seen the Lord. Thomas would not have it. Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe. He set terms. He named the exact proof he wanted, down to where his finger would go.

Eight days pass, and John tells you nothing about them. Then his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Doors locked again. Jesus comes again. Peace again. Then He turns to one man: Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. He uses Thomas’ own words back to him. He had heard every syllable of that refusal, and He did not come to shame him. He came to meet him. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.

John never says Thomas touched Him. He says Thomas answered: My Lord and my God. It is the highest confession in the Gospel, out of the mouth of the man who held out longest. The book that opened with the Word was God reaches its summit with a man calling Jesus God to His face — and Jesus takes it. He does not correct him. He receives worship that belongs to God alone, because He is God, the Word made flesh, wounds and all.

Then Jesus looks past the room: Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed. That is you. You will never see the hands. You will not get Thomas’ second meeting. You get what Jesus calls blessed — faith resting on His word without sight. Thomas did not get a better deal than you.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: THAT YOU MAY BELIEVE
paras: Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. John was choosing. He saw more than he set down. What he put in front of you was picked with care, the way a mason picks stones for a hearth — not every rock in the field, only the ones that will bear the fire. Then he tells you why: but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

That sentence is the key to everything this series has walked through. Water turned to wine at Cana, and his disciples believed in him. An official heard Go your way. Your son lives, and walked home trusting a word. A man thirty-eight years sick took up his mat. Five thousand ate from a boy’s lunch. Frightened men on a dark sea heard It is I. Don’t be afraid. A man born blind washed in Siloam and came back seeing. Lazarus walked out of the grave. Each sign was a finger pointing at one Man.

And the aim was never to make you a better-informed spectator. John wrote that you may believe — trust yourself to Jesus as the Christ the prophets promised and the Son who shares the Father’s life. And believing, have life. Not a wage for a faith strong enough. Life given in His name, held now: the man who believes has eternal life (5:24).
Thomas needed the wounds. You have the book, and John says it is enough. The God who gave the signs gave the record of them, and the Spirit breathed out in that room still opens eyes to read it.

stations.verse: When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle, and said to them, “Peace be to you.
stations.question: Jesus came through the locked doors of men who had deserted Him, and His first word was Peace be to you; what fear have I bolted myself in with this week that I need Him to speak peace into?
stations.gloss: to shut; to lock
body: Kleiō means to shut — a door, a prison, the gates of a city. In a figure it can mean shutting the sky so no rain falls, or shutting the heart against a brother in need. It turns up in 15 New Testament verses, and John uses it twice, both of this same room.
The doors were shut for fear of the Jews. And Jesus came and stood in the middle. The door did not keep Him out, and their fear did not make Him angry. He carried peace into the shut room.

The dust wants you to believe a shut door settles it — that fear or shame can lock Christ out for good. Revelation names Him as the One who opens and no one can shut. What He has opened to you no one can close, and the door you bolted from the inside is no wall to Him.
stations.live: Name the fear that has you bolted in this week. Each morning, with your hand on the front door, say: ‘He came through the locked door with peace. He comes through this one too.’

stations.verse: The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.
stations.question: The others told Thomas We have seen the Lord, and he would not believe without the nail prints under his own finger; what proof on my own terms am I still demanding before I rest on their witness to Christ?
stations.gloss: a nail
body: Hēlos means a nail, the kind a carpenter drives. In the Greek Old Testament it shows up in Isaiah, where a craftsman fastens it with nails, that it might not totter — an idol propped up by human hands. In the New Testament it stands in one verse only, and it falls to a doubting man to say it.
Thomas did not ask for a glow or a voice. He asked for the marks of the nails. The proof he named was the cross itself, carried in the risen body.

The dust says your faith needs fresh proof every week. Thomas got his proof, and it was the same wounds that had already paid for him. Isaiah said it long before: by his wounds we are healed. An idol needs nails to keep it standing. The living Christ bears nail marks because He stood in your place.
stations.live: When doubt comes this week, do not demand a new sign. Go back to the old wounds. Read John 20:25–27 and say: ‘The hands that took the nails are alive. That is enough for me.’

stations.verse: Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.
stations.question: Jesus came back for Thomas, held out the very wounds he had demanded, and said Don’t be unbelieving, but believing; what doubt have I kept from Christ, as if He would turn me away for it?
stations.gloss: unbelieving; without faith or trust
body: Apistos is the word for believing, pistos, with a negative set in front of it. Said of a thing, it means hard to believe — Paul asks King Agrippa why anyone should find it so that God raises the dead. Said of a man, it means one without faith or trust. It appears in 21 New Testament verses.

In Mark, Jesus sighs over an Unbelieving generation. With Thomas He uses the same word, but He says it with His hands held out. He does not stand off and wait for Thomas to fix himself. He comes to him, offers the wounds, and calls him out of unbelief into faith.

The dust tells you doubt means you are finished. Jesus did not shut Thomas out. He came back for him. His word to Thomas was a call, and the call carried its own power. Thomas answered, My Lord and my God.
stations.live: Write down the doubt you have been ashamed to say out loud. Bring it to Christ in plain words. Then read 20:27–28 and answer Him the way Thomas did: ‘My Lord and my God.’

stations.verse: Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book.
stations.question: John admits that many other signs were left out of his book, so what he wrote was chosen and enough; where am I asking God for more than the Scripture He has already put in my hands?
stations.gloss: a book, a scroll; a written document
body: Biblion means a written thing — a legal paper, a scroll, a book. The certificate of divorce Moses allowed is a biblion. So is the scroll of Isaiah handed to Jesus in Nazareth. The word appears in 29 New Testament verses, and Revelation speaks more than once of the book of life.
John calls his Gospel this book and admits it is not the whole story. Jesus did many other signs that John left out. What remained was chosen for one work. It holds enough to give a man life.

The dust says you need more than the page — a dream, a feeling, a word nobody else has heard. John says the book is enough. And there is another book behind this one. Revelation says the only ones who enter the holy city are those who are written in the Lamb’s book of life. Every man who believes in Him is written there.
stations.live: Read one chapter of John each day this week before you look at a screen. Before you start, say: ‘This was written that I may believe. Let it do its work in me.’

stations.verse: But these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.
stations.question: John wrote so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and have life in His name; what am I still leaning on for life beside that name?
stations.gloss: to believe; to trust in, rely on
body: Pisteuō means to believe. John’s Gospel uses it in 85 verses, out of 217 in the New Testament. Often it comes with a small word that makes it believing in or on someone — not only granting that a thing is true, but trusting yourself to a person.

That is the faith 20:31 calls for: your whole weight leaned on Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God. John does not write so you will admire Him. He writes so you will rest on Him. And the promise is not a reward for strong faith. It is life in his name, received by an empty hand.

The dust wants faith to be one more work, a muscle you must build before God pays out. Jesus said, This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. He gives the right to become God’s children to those who believe in his name.
stations.live: Write 20:31 on a card and keep it in your wallet. When the week tells you to earn your place, pull it out and say: ‘I believe Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and I have life in His name.’

practices.title: OPEN THE BOLTED DOOR
practices.body: Name the fear that has you shut in — the call you will not make, the conversation with your wife you keep putting off, the doctor’s appointment you keep moving. Read John 20:19–21 on Monday morning. Peace was His first word to frightened men, and He said it before they did one brave thing. Then do the thing fear has been holding back. Do it this week, as a man the risen Lord has already spoken peace over.

practices.title: GO WHERE YOU ARE SENT
practices.body: As the Father has sent me, even so I send you. You were not sent on your own breath; He breathed out the Spirit first. Pick one man this week — someone on your crew, the neighbor across the fence, your brother-in-law — and tell him plainly what Christ has done: every sin of the man who believes in Him is forgiven. No speech. A few true sentences over coffee or across a tailgate, and leave the rest to the Spirit.

practices.title: BRING YOUR DOUBT TO HIS WOUNDS
practices.body: Thomas said his doubt out loud, and Jesus answered it to his face. Write down the question that keeps you up — the one you are ashamed to ask at church. Then read Isaiah 53:5 and John 20:24–29 slowly. Do not ask for a new sign. Set your doubt beside the wounds that paid for you and the Lord who came back for one stubborn man. Tell one trusted brother what you wrote.

practices.title: SAY THOMAS’ CONFESSION
practices.body: Each morning before your boots are on, say it aloud: My Lord and my God. Then name one thing that confession reaches today. Lord means He gives the orders — over the money, the phone, the way you talk to your boy. God means He gets the worship, not your work or your name. Thomas was not working up a feeling. He was telling the truth about who stood in front of him. Do the same.

practices.title: READ THE BOOK IT WAS WRITTEN FOR
practices.body: John says his book was written that you may believe. This week read John 1–11 in four sittings — a few chapters at a time, at lunch or after supper. Put a mark beside each sign, and write one line under it: what this shows me about who Jesus is. On Sunday, read 20:30–31 again and thank God that the book did what He wrote it to do.

title: My Lord and My God
subtitle: from dust to faith that has not seen
keyVerse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!

passage.text: When therefore it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and when the doors were locked where the disciples were assembled, for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the middle, and said to them, “Peace be to you.”
When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. The disciples therefore were glad when they saw the Lord.
Jesus therefore said to them again, “Peace be to you. As the Father has sent me, even so I send you.”
When he had said this, he breathed on them, and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit!
If you forgive anyone’s sins, they have been forgiven them. If you retain anyone’s sins, they have been retained.”
But Thomas, one of the twelve, called Didymus, wasn’t with them when Jesus came.

The other disciples therefore said to him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the print of the nails, put my finger into the print of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.”
After eight days again his disciples were inside and Thomas was with them. Jesus came, the doors being locked, and stood in the middle, and said, “Peace be to you.”
Then he said to Thomas, “Reach here your finger, and see my hands. Reach here your hand, and put it into my side. Don’t be unbelieving, but believing.”
Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!”
Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.”
Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book;
but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.

stationsIntro: Five words carry you from a bolted door to the sentence John wrote his whole Gospel for. Read each verse, answer it plainly, and let the Greek send you back to the risen Christ who meets doubters with His wounds.
lifeIntro: Behind a locked door the risen Christ spoke peace to frightened men, and a week later He came back for one doubter. Then He blessed every man who would believe without seeing, and John wrote his book so you could be that man. These practices are how a man takes Him at His word.
lifePulls: Faith that has not seen is not second-class faith. Jesus called it blessed, and John wrote a whole book to give it to you. The risen Christ who met Thomas in that room meets you on the page.
prayer: Father, Your Son came through locked doors and said peace to frightened men. He showed them His hands and His side, and those wounds tell me my sin was paid for. He breathed on them and gave the Holy Spirit; give me that same Spirit as I read Your word. He came back for Thomas, and He has come back for me more times than I can count. Forgive my unbelief, and the terms I have set for You. Jesus is my Lord and my God; let Him rule my house, my money and my mouth this week. Thank You for the blessing spoken over those who have not seen and have believed. Let this book do its work in me, that I may believe and have life in His name. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: On the evening of the first day, the risen Christ walked into a locked room, said peace, and showed His wounds. He sent His men out with His Spirit and His gospel. A week later He came back for Thomas, met his terms, and heard the plainest confession in the book: My Lord and my God. Then He blessed the man who believes without seeing. John wrote the whole Gospel so that man could have life. That man is you.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, to the One standing in the middle of a locked room. He stands there with the bolt still thrown. He stands there with the print of the nails in His hands and the mark of the spear in His side. He stands there alive, the same Jesus who was laid in the tomb, and the first word out of His mouth is peace. You did not open the door for Him. You were hiding behind it.

Look at what John has put in your hands to bring you to that room. He did not write down everything; he tells you many other signs went unrecorded. What he kept, he kept on purpose — the Word who was God made flesh, the signs that showed His glory, the cross, the empty tomb, the locked room and the wounds. He chose every page with one man in mind, and the man is you: that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.

You have not seen what Thomas saw. You will never put your finger in the print of the nails. But you are not left outside with second-hand faith. The same Lord who came back eight days later for one stubborn man has spoken a blessing over every man like you: Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed. Your doubts did not catch Him off guard. He met Thomas’ doubts with His own wounds, and He meets yours with the same wounds, set down in this book for you to read.

So take Thomas’ words for your own this week, at the job and at your own door: my Lord and my God. It is not a feeling to wait for. It is a confession to make, because it is true. The wounds are real. The tomb is empty. The Spirit has been breathed out. And the promise at the end of John’s book is not a wage but a gift: believing, you may have life in his name. That life is yours on Tuesday, in the dust, because the One with nail-scarred hands is alive, and no one will snatch you out of them.
closingVerse: Thomas answered him, “My Lord and my God!
carry: Thomas saw the wounds and said My Lord and my God, and Jesus blessed every man who would believe without seeing; where in your week will you confess Him as your Lord and your God without waiting to see?

sections.heading: Where the Dust Lies to You
paras: The dust keeps a record of your worst night. It does not forget the words you said, the door you walked out of, the moment you went quiet when it was your turn to stand. It plays the tape back at odd hours — on the drive home, in the shower, when the house goes still. And every time, it adds the same note at the bottom: that is who you really are.

Then it tells you what follows. A man who failed like that can be forgiven, maybe, but he cannot be trusted again. He can sit in the back row. He can keep his head down and stay out of the way. But the work, the trust, the charge to care for anyone else’s soul — those belong to men with cleaner records. So you go back to what you knew before — the work you can measure, the tools that do not ask questions. You go back to the nets.

Lay an old prayer beside that record: My soul clings to the dust; Revive me according to Your word. (NKJV) It does not ask God to pretend the night never happened. It asks Him to raise a man off the floor, and to do it by speaking. That is how God has always raised dust: by a word.

John 21 is that word, spoken over the man who failed worst. Peter denied Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire. Here, beside another charcoal fire, the risen Christ feeds him breakfast, asks him three times, hands him the sheep, and says Follow me.

sections.heading: Back to the Sea
pulls: The dust says a man who failed like that can be forgiven but never trusted again. Jesus built a fire, cooked the fish, asked three questions, and put His own sheep in that man’s hands.
paras: John 20 ended with what sounds like a closing line: these are written, that you may believe. Then John takes up the pen once more. The scene moves to the sea of Tiberias — the Sea of Galilee, where Matthew tells you Peter and the sons of Zebedee were working the nets when Jesus first called them. Peter is there again, with Thomas, Nathanael of Cana, the sons of Zebedee, and two others. They fish all night and catch nothing. At daybreak a man on the beach tells them where to cast.

This is the last chapter of the last volume in this series. Four volumes have walked you from In the beginning was the Word to a breakfast on a Galilee beach. The chapter closes with the writer himself, vouching for his witness and admitting the world could not hold the whole story. Read 21:1–25 in one sitting. Watch what the risen Lord does with a man who failed Him, and then ask what He means to do with you.

parts.label: PART ONE
parts.heading: A NIGHT OF EMPTY NETS
paras: Peter says I’m going fishing, and six others go with him. John does not tell you why, and you should not guess. He tells you the result: That night, they caught nothing. Men who knew the water, the right boat, the whole night, and an empty net hauled in again and again.

But when day had already come, Jesus stood on the beach, yet the disciples didn’t know that it was Jesus. He calls across the water with a question He already knows the answer to: Children, have you anything to eat? They answer with one word, and the whole night is in it: No. Then He tells them, Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some. They do, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.

Like every sign in John, the catch points to a Person. The disciple whom Jesus loved sees it first: It’s the Lord. And Peter — the man who denied Him three times — wrapped his coat around himself and threw himself into the sea. He does not wait for the boat. Whatever he carried out of that courtyard, he swims toward Jesus, not away from Him.

The others bring the boat in, dragging the net full of fish. The haul came at the Lord’s word, not by their skill. Your work this week is real work, and you should do it well — the fuel bill and the feed order do not pay themselves. But the full net is His gift. The One who gives it is the point, and He is standing on the beach.

parts.label: PART TWO
parts.heading: BREAKFAST BY A CHARCOAL FIRE
paras: So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it. John uses a word here he has used only once before. The last fire of coals in this Gospel burned in the high priest’s courtyard, and Peter stood beside it warming himself while he denied he ever knew Jesus. Now Jesus has built one on the beach. He does not bring Peter back to the place of his failure to rub his face in it. He brings him to a fire with breakfast on it.

The fish are already cooking, and still He says, Bring some of the fish which you have just caught. He wants their catch at His fire. Peter drags the net ashore, full of one hundred fifty-three great fish, and John adds that the net wasn’t torn. Somebody counted. Do not hunt for a hidden code in the number; John gives you a tally, not a riddle.

Then the invitation: Come and eat breakfast. None of the disciples dared inquire of him, John says, knowing that it was the Lord. And Jesus came and took the bread, gave it to them, and the fish likewise. The hands that once fed five thousand by this same sea. The hands with the print of the nails. The Lord of glory serves breakfast to men who scattered the night He was taken.

This is now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples after he had risen from the dead. He keeps coming to them. Grace does not make one visit and leave the rest to you. Before He says one word about Peter’s failure, He feeds him.

parts.label: PART THREE
parts.heading: THREE QUESTIONS
pulls: Three times Peter denied Him in a courtyard where a fire of coals burned. Three times Jesus asked him beside another, and gave him the sheep after every answer. That is what the risen Christ does with a man’s worst night.
paras: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus turns to one man. Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these? He uses the name Peter had before Jesus renamed him (1:42). Peter had once said I will lay down my life for you. Now he says only, Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you. No comparison with the others. No vow. He leans on what Jesus knows.

Jesus asks a second time, and a third, and Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time. Three denials by one fire; three questions by another. Jesus does not skip the hard part, and He does not leave Peter in it. He is not grinding Peter down. He is giving him a confession for every denial, so the old record is met point for point. The grief is the grief of a wound being cleaned, not torn open again.

Two different verbs for love run through these verses. Jesus asks twice with one; Peter answers each time with the other, which the WEB renders have affection for; and the third time Jesus takes up Peter’s word. Do not build a ladder out of that. John uses Peter’s word for the Father’s love of the Son (5:20) and for the Father’s love of you (16:27). The weight falls elsewhere: three questions for three denials, and a charge after every answer.

Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you. That is where a restored man stands — on the Lord who knows him through and through, the courtyard included, and asks anyway. Each answer gets its reply: Feed my lambs, Tend my sheep, Feed my sheep. The sheep are His. He hands them to the man who denied Him.

parts.label: PART FOUR
parts.heading: YOU FOLLOW ME
paras: Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go. John explains it: he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. The man who swore he would die for Jesus and then folded before a doorkeeper will one day die for Him in fact — kept by grace, not by nerve. And the next word is Follow me.

Peter turns and sees the disciple whom Jesus loved. Lord, what about this man? The answer is blunt: If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me. Your road is not your brother’s. You will not be asked to account for his. Christ will see to that man. Your part is the next step behind Him. John even corrects a rumor about himself; Jesus never said that disciple would not die.

This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true. The writer, known to the church as John the son of Zebedee, signs off as a witness. Then the last line: There are also many other things which Jesus did, so many that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.

Four volumes, twenty-one chapters, and you have barely touched the hem. The story of Jesus does not run out. It goes on in every lamb fed and every brother restored, and in every forgiven man who hears Follow me and gets up from the fire.

stations.verse: He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.
stations.question: After a night of nothing, the net filled at a stranger’s word from the beach, and the beloved disciple said It’s the Lord; what good thing in my work have I been crediting to my own skill instead of to Him?
stations.gloss: a net
body: Diktyon is the plain word for a net. It shows up in 11 New Testament verses, every one of them on the Sea of Galilee. Matthew uses it on the day Jesus first called Peter and Andrew: They immediately left their nets and followed him.

Luke tells of an earlier morning when Peter said, we worked all night, and took nothing, then let down the net at Jesus’ word and their net was breaking. Now, after the cross and the empty tomb, it happens again — an empty night, a word from Jesus, a net too full to haul.

The dust tells you the net is yours: your skill, your hours, and your empty nights to explain away. The full net says the catch belonged to the One on the beach. You still cast. But you cast at His word, and the haul is a gift that points back to Him.
stations.live: Before work each day this week, hand the day to the Lord in one sentence. At quitting time, name one thing that came in you did not earn, and say: ‘That was from the Lord on the beach.’

stations.verse: So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it.
stations.question: Peter denied Jesus while warming himself at a charcoal fire, and the risen Christ called him to breakfast at a fire He had ready; what old failure of mine is Christ meeting with bread instead of accusation?
stations.gloss: a charcoal fire; a heap of burning coals
body: Anthrakia means a heap of burning coals, a charcoal fire. The New Testament uses it in two verses only, and John wrote both of them.

The first is 18:18, the night of the arrest. The servants and officers stood having made a fire of coals, for it was cold, and Peter stood with them, warming himself, saying I am not. The second is here on the beach, where Jesus has built the fire Himself, with fish and bread laid on it. The same kind of fire, a different host. And Peter swam to this one.

The dust drags you back to the fire where you failed and leaves you there in the cold. Christ brings you back to a fire too, but He is the One tending it, and the first thing He does is feed you. He does not pretend the first fire never burned. He answers it.
stations.live: Name the night your worst failure is tied to. Read John 18:18 and 21:9 side by side, then say: ‘He built a second fire. He met me there with bread, not a charge sheet.’

stations.verse: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.
stations.question: Peter once vowed I will lay down my life for you; now he answers only you know that I have affection for you; where does my love for Christ still lean on my vows instead of His knowing me?
stations.gloss: to love as a friend, have affection for; to kiss
body: Phileō means to love with the warmth of friendship; it can also mean to kiss, as in the kiss Judas gave. It appears in 21 New Testament verses, three of them in 21:15–17. Here the WEB renders it have affection for.

Do not hang too much on the difference. John uses phileō for the Father’s love of the Son, and for the Father’s love of you: for the Father himself loves you. The weight here is on the ground Peter stands on. He no longer offers a vow. He rests on what Jesus knows.

The dust says your love for Christ has to be big enough to outweigh your failures. Peter’s answer makes no such claim. The Lord who knows everything knew the denials and asked anyway. Your love for Him starts there — in being fully known and still called.
stations.live: Stop trying to prove your love to Christ with fresh vows this week. Each morning, pray Peter’s words as your own: ‘Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.’

stations.verse: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.
stations.question: Each time Peter answered, Jesus gave him no penance but a charge, Feed my lambs; whose soul has Christ put within my reach to feed with His word this week?
stations.gloss: to feed, as a herdsman feeds his flock
body: Boskō is a herdsman’s word: to feed animals, to put them out to graze. It occurs in 9 New Testament verses, and most of them are about pigs — among them the far country, where the lost son was sent into his fields to feed pigs. Only in John 21 is it used of feeding Christ’s people.

Jesus says it twice: Feed my lambs and Feed my sheep. Between them He says Tend my sheep, a wider word that takes in oversight as well. Feeding sits at the heart of it. Peter’s love would show itself in feeding Christ’s flock.

The dust tells a restored man to keep his head down and stay clear of anyone else’s soul. Jesus did the opposite. He took the man who had failed worst and put the lambs in his hands. The Good Shepherd laid down His life for the sheep, and He still feeds them through forgiven men.
stations.live: Pick one person Christ has put near you — your son, a younger man at work, your wife. This week open John with him for ten minutes and say: ‘These are His sheep. He told me to feed them.’

stations.verse: Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go.
stations.question: Jesus told Peter that following Him would end in a death that would glorify God, then said Follow me; what cost am I holding back from that call, as if my Restorer could not be trusted with my end?
stations.gloss: to gird; to dress
body: Zōnnymi means to gird, to fasten your clothes about you. The WEB says dressed. Only two New Testament verses use it, and both are about Peter.

Here Jesus says young Peter dressed himself and went where he wanted, but old Peter would stretch out your hands, and another will dress you. John explains it was the death by which Peter would glorify God. The other verse is Acts 12, where Peter sleeps in chains and an angel tells him, Get dressed and put on your sandals, and leads him out of prison.

The dust says that if following Christ costs you your own way, He must not be good. Jesus told Peter the cost in plain words and then said Follow me. He did not lure him with half the story. Another would dress Peter for the end, but the One who said Follow me had walked that road ahead of him.
stations.live: Each morning as you buckle your belt, pray: ‘You dress me now, Lord, and You will dress me at the end. Wherever You lead me, I will follow.’

practices.title: EAT BEFORE YOU WORK
practices.body: Jesus fed Peter before He said one word about the courtyard. Before you try to make anything right this week, sit with what Christ has already done. On Monday, read John 21:9–14 slowly at the start of the day. Picture the fire and the bread in His hands. Then thank Him for one specific mercy He has given you without your asking. A man who has been fed does not work to earn the meal.

practices.title: BRING THE OLD FIRE TO THE NEW ONE
practices.body: Name the failure you keep replaying — the denial, the betrayal, the night you walked out. Write it down in plain words. Then read John 18:15–27 and 21:15–17 back to back. Confess it to God, and if a brother or your wife needs to hear it from you, tell them this week. Then tear up the paper and burn it. The Lord met Peter at the second fire, and He meets you there.

practices.title: ANSWER ON HIS KNOWLEDGE
practices.body: Peter did not make another vow. He said, Lord, you know everything. When accusation comes this week — about the temper, the second drink, the money you hid — do not answer with promises to do better. Answer with what Christ knows: He knows all of it, He went to the cross for all of it, and He still calls you. Say it plainly, out loud, in the cab or out by the barn.

practices.title: FEED ONE LAMB
practices.body: Feed my lambs was the first charge Jesus gave a restored man. Pick one person this week who needs the word of Christ — your son, a younger man on the night shift, a neighbor in a hard season. Sit down with him twice. Open John and read a chapter together. Do not lecture, and do not wait until you feel qualified. Feed. The sheep are Christ’s, and He has trusted you with one.

practices.title: FOLLOW WITHOUT COMPARING
practices.body: What is that to you? You follow me. Name the man whose road you keep measuring yours against — his health, his marriage, his easy faith, his bigger shop. Every time the comparison comes up this week, stop and say the words back to yourself. His road is in His hands, and so is yours. Then do the next plain thing Christ has put in front of you: the job, the phone call, the bedtime prayer with your kids.

title: Do You Love Me?
subtitle: from dust to a fisherman restored
keyVerse: He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

passage.text: After these things, Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples at the sea of Tiberias. He revealed himself this way.
Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael of Cana in Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.
Simon Peter said to them, “I’m going fishing.” They told him, “We are also coming with you.” They immediately went out, and entered into the boat. That night, they caught nothing.
But when day had already come, Jesus stood on the beach, yet the disciples didn’t know that it was Jesus.
Jesus therefore said to them, “Children, have you anything to eat?” They answered him, “No.”
He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” They cast it therefore, and now they weren’t able to draw it in for the multitude of fish.

That disciple therefore whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It’s the Lord!” So when Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he wrapped his coat around himself (for he was naked), and threw himself into the sea.
But the other disciples came in the little boat (for they were not far from the land, but about two hundred cubits away), dragging the net full of fish.
So when they got out on the land, they saw a fire of coals there, with fish and bread laid on it.
Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish which you have just caught.”
Simon Peter went up, and drew the net to land, full of one hundred fifty-three great fish. Even though there were so many, the net wasn’t torn.
Jesus said to them, “Come and eat breakfast!” None of the disciples dared inquire of him, “Who are you?” knowing that it was the Lord.
Then Jesus came and took the bread, gave it to them, and the fish likewise.
This is now the third time that Jesus was revealed to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.

So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.”
He said to him again a second time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.” He said to him, “Tend my sheep.”

He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?” Peter was grieved because he asked him the third time, “Do you have affection for me?” He said to him, “Lord, you know everything. You know that I have affection for you.” Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep.

Most certainly I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted to. But when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you don’t want to go.”
Now he said this, signifying by what kind of death he would glorify God. When he had said this, he said to him, “Follow me.”
Then Peter, turning around, saw a disciple following. This was the disciple whom Jesus loved, the one who had also leaned on Jesus’ breast at the supper and asked, “Lord, who is going to betray you?”
Peter seeing him, said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”
Jesus said to him, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.”

This saying therefore went out among the brothers, that this disciple wouldn’t die. Yet Jesus didn’t say to him that he wouldn’t die, but, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you?”
This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true.
There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.

stationsIntro: Five words carry you from an empty net to the last command Jesus gives in John’s Gospel. Read each verse, answer it plainly, and let the Greek bring you back to the fire where the risen Lord restores His men.
lifeIntro: On a Galilee beach the risen Christ built the fire, cooked the fish, and called the man who had denied Him to breakfast. Then He answered three denials with three questions and three charges. These practices are for a man who has been fed at that fire and told to follow.
lifePulls: Christ does not restore a man halfway. He feeds him, faces the failure with him, hears his confession, hands him work, and says Follow me. The man who denied Him would one day die glorifying God.
prayer: Father, Your Son stood on the beach while His men caught nothing, and He called them children. He built a fire and fed men who had scattered from Him. He asked Peter three times and gave him the sheep after every answer. Lord, You know everything about me, the cold nights and the denials included. Thank You that You restore us and do not merely put up with us. Give me a love that rests on Your knowing me, not on my promises. Put lambs in front of me this week, and make me faithful to feed them with Your word. When I look sideways at another man’s road, turn my eyes back to Christ, who says Follow me. Keep me believing, that I may have life in His name to the end. In Jesus’ name, amen.

bottomLine: Peter denied Jesus three times by a charcoal fire. After the empty tomb, the risen Lord filled his net, built another fire, cooked him breakfast, and asked him three times, do you love me? Three answers, three charges: feed My sheep. Then Jesus told Peter how he would die, and said Follow me. The man who failed worst was not shelved. He was fed, restored and sent, and so are you.
benediction: Lift up your eyes, dusty soul, and look back down the whole road John has walked you. See the Word who was with God and was God, made flesh and living among men, full of grace and truth. See the water turned to wine at Cana, a father’s son alive by a word, a man thirty-eight years sick walking home with his mat. See bread for five thousand, a blind man washing mud from his eyes, and Lazarus coming out at the sound of his name. Every sign was His glory shining through dust.

Hear Him say who He is. I am the bread of life. I am the light of the world. I am the door, and I am the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. I am the resurrection and the life. I am the way, the truth, and the life. Then see Him step out to meet the soldiers in the garden. See Him lifted up on the cross, and hear It is finished. See the stone taken away and the cloths lying in an empty tomb. Hear Mary called by name, and Thomas cry My Lord and my God.

And then the beach. The man who denied Him three times by one fire is fed beside another, asked three times, and three times handed the sheep. That is where this Gospel lands — not on a man who held on, but on a Christ who would not let go of the man who didn’t. If He did that for Peter, He has not given up on you. Your worst night is not the last word over your life. His word is.

So rise from the fire, dusty soul, fed and forgiven. John wrote all of it that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name. That life is not a loan you must keep paying on. It is yours now, given in His name and held in hands that still bear the nails. When you stumble this week, He will not hand you back your worst night. He will do what He did on that beach. He will feed you, ask for your heart, put His work in your hands, and go ahead of you. And the last word the risen Christ speaks to a restored man in this book is the word He speaks to you at the back door with your boots laced: Follow me.
